lead: Isaiah looks at a felled royal house and sees one green shoot, on whom the Spirit of the Lord will rest, and around whom creation itself will be at peace. In Luke that future arrives: Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and tells his disciples that their eyes are seeing what prophets and kings longed to see. The first reading is the longing of Advent; the Gospel says the waiting has not been in vain.

r.h: A shoot from the stump of Jesse
set: Isaiah prophesied in Judah in the eighth century BC, when Assyria was swallowing the small kingdoms around it and the kings of David's line were often a disappointment. Chapter 10 has just ended with the image of a great forest cut down by the Lord. Chapter 11 begins with what grows after the axe: hope comes where everything looks finished.
str: v. 1: the shoot and the branch.
vv. 2–3a: the Spirit who rests on him.
vv. 3b–5: his justice, above all for the poor.
vv. 6–9: peace among the animals and on the holy mountain.
v. 10: the root of Jesse as a signal to the nations.
kw: What remains of a felled tree. Isaiah says the stump of Jesse, not of David. God goes back behind the palace to the shepherd family of Bethlehem and begins again.
A green shoot. Many interpreters hear this word behind Matthew's saying that Jesus “will be called a Nazorean” (Matthew 2:23), though Matthew does not explain it.
The same word means breath and wind. The king's power will not be his own army but the breath of God resting on him.
vv: A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots.
God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7) survives the failure of David's sons. The stump looks dead, but the root is alive.
The spirit of the Lord shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord.
The Hebrew names six gifts, and “fear of the Lord” comes again in v. 3. The Greek and Latin versions render the first “fear” as “piety”, and so the Church came to count seven gifts.
The wolf shall live with the lamb, the leopard shall lie down with the kid

This is poetry about a world healed at its root, with the harmony of Eden restored. The reason follows in v. 9: the earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord. Where God is known, no one needs to hurt anyone.
ch: The Catechism sees in these verses the features of the promised Messiah, on whom the Spirit rests (CCC 712), and draws from them its teaching on the seven gifts, which “belong in their fullness to Christ, Son of David” (CCC 1831). St Paul quotes v. 10 to show that the nations too hope in Christ (Romans 15:12). St Jerome, playing on the Latin virga (shoot) and virgo (virgin), took the shoot as Mary and the flower that rises from it as Christ (in substance).

r.h: The eyes that see
set: The disciples have just come back from their mission full of joy (10:17–20). Jesus tells them to rejoice that their names are written in heaven. Then he himself rejoices. Matthew has the same saying (Matthew 11:25–27), but only Luke tells us of the joy and of the Holy Spirit.
str: v. 21: Jesus' prayer of thanks to the Father.
v. 22: the unique knowledge between the Father and the Son.
vv. 23–24: a private blessing on the disciples.
kw: A strong word for exultant, festive joy. Luke uses it of Mary's spirit in the Magnificat (1:47). Here the joy of Jesus is the joy of the Holy Spirit.
Little ones who cannot yet speak well. They are the disciples, simple people who receive what the learned refuse. Jesus is not praising ignorance, but the open hand.
vv: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants
The whole Trinity appears in one verse: the Son rejoices in the Holy Spirit and gives thanks to the Father. The shoot of Isaiah, on whom the Spirit rests, is praying.
no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.
To “know” here means a shared life and not only information. We know the Father only because the Son lets us into what he himself has with the Father.
Blessed are the eyes that see what you see!
The prophets, Isaiah among them, saw from far away (compare Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 1:10–12). The disciples are looking at the promise itself.
ch: The Catechism counts this among the two explicit prayers of Jesus preserved from his public ministry, and notes that each begins with thanksgiving (CCC 2603). It also cites the parallel in Matthew when it teaches that Jesus revealed God as Father in an unheard-of sense (CCC 240). The Church's Advent is a school for such little ones: the Lord who came is known by those who receive him as a gift.

qa: Are there six gifts of the Holy Spirit in Isaiah, or seven?

The Hebrew text of 11:2–3 names six and mentions the fear of the Lord twice. The Greek and Latin translations gave the first mention as “piety”, which gives seven. The Church's list of seven (CCC 1831) rests on that long reading of the text. Seven also suggests fullness, which is the point: the Spirit rests on the Messiah without measure, and we share his gifts.
study: Where in my life or my family does the stump look dead? What would it mean to look there for a shoot?
Jesus thanks the Father for revealing himself to “infants”. What keeps me from receiving God's word like one of them?

lead: On a mountain the Lord spreads a feast for all peoples and swallows up death forever. In Matthew, Jesus goes up a mountain and sits down; the crowds lay their sick at his feet, and he feeds them until they are filled. Advent's hope has a table in it, and the Gospel shows who the host is.

r.h: A feast for all peoples
set: Isaiah 24–27 is often called the “Isaiah Apocalypse”, because it looks beyond the fall of particular cities to God's final victory over the whole earth. Scholars generally think it was given its present form later than the eighth-century prophet. The reading is a hymn set on “this mountain”, which is Zion, the mountain of the Temple.
str: v. 6: the banquet.
vv. 7–8: the shroud removed, death swallowed, tears wiped away.
vv. 9–10a: the song of those who waited.
kw: A banquet, from the verb “to drink”. In the ancient East a covenant or a king's enthronement was sealed with a meal. God himself is the host here, and the guest list has no borders.
A covering, perhaps the mourner's veil. The covering over all peoples is death and the grief that goes with it.
In the old poems of Canaan, Death was pictured as a monster with an endless throat. Here the swallower is swallowed.
vv: On this mountain the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wines
“All peoples” is the key. Israel's God is the host, and the mountain of Israel becomes the table of the nations.
he will swallow up death forever. Then the Lord God will wipe away the tears from all faces

St Paul quotes the first words about the resurrection: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54). The book of Revelation takes up the tears (Revelation 7:17; 21:4). God wipes them with his own hand.
This is the Lord for whom we have waited; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation.
This is the song of Advent. “Waiting” is not an empty time; it ends in recognition: “Lo, this is our God.”
ch: The Church hears this banquet in the Eucharist, which the Catechism calls a pledge of the glory to come and an anticipation of the heavenly feast (CCC 1402–1405). It reads the wiping of tears together with Revelation when it speaks of the new universe, in which God will dwell among us (CCC 1044). “All peoples” remains the Church's horizon: the Gospel excludes no one.

r.h: Seven loaves on the mountain
set: Jesus has just healed the daughter of a Canaanite woman in the region of Tyre and Sidon (15:21–28). Now he comes back to the Sea of Galilee. Mark places the parallel scene in the region of the Decapolis, Gentile territory (Mark 7:31; 8:1–10), and many read Matthew's crowd in that light, since they praise “the God of Israel”. Matthew has already told a first feeding (14:13–21).
str: vv. 29–31: on the mountain: the sick at his feet; the crowd amazed.
vv. 32–34: Jesus' compassion; the disciples' question; “How many loaves?”
vv. 35–37: the crowd seated; thanks, breaking, giving; seven baskets left over.
kw: From the word for the inner organs: to be moved in one's depths. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus, or of figures in his parables who stand for God.
Matthew's word here (v. 36), from which our word Eucharist comes. In the first feeding he wrote “blessed” (14:19).
vv: Great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the maimed, the blind, the mute, and many others. They put them at his feet, and he cured them,
Jesus sits on a mountain as he did to teach (5:1). What Isaiah promised for the mountain of God now begins around him.
I have compassion for the crowd, because they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat
Here Jesus starts the conversation. He sees the hunger before anyone mentions it.
he took the seven loaves and the fish; and after giving thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

The four verbs (took, gave thanks, broke, gave) return at the Last Supper (26:26–27). The disciples, who asked where bread could be found, become the hands that serve it. Then “all of them ate and were filled” (15:37), and what remains is more than what they began with.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the multiplication of the loaves prefigures “the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist” (CCC 1335). Some of the Fathers saw in the two feedings of the Gospels the two peoples called to one table, Israel and the nations (in substance). At every Mass the same four actions are done, and the same people are fed: those who could not feed themselves.

qa: Did the crowd simply share what they had brought, or was it a miracle?

The text says plainly that seven loaves and a few fish fed the whole crowd, that all were filled, and that seven baskets were left. All four Evangelists tell a feeding of this kind as a sign of Jesus' power, and the Church reads it so (CCC 1335). Sharing is a real lesson of the scene, but it is the fruit of the miracle, not an explanation of it.
study: Isaiah says God will wipe the tears “from all faces”. Whose tears can I help to wipe this Advent?
The disciples had only seven loaves. What small thing do I hold back from Jesus because it seems too little?

lead: Isaiah sings of a strong city whose walls are God's own saving work, and he gives the reason it stands: “in the Lord God you have an everlasting rock.” Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with two houses in one storm, and the rock now has a practical meaning: hearing his words and doing them. Advent is a good time to look at the foundations.

r.h: The everlasting rock
set: This song belongs to the same section as yesterday's feast (Isaiah 24–27). Two cities stand side by side there: the proud city that falls and the city of those who trust. Ancient people felt safe behind high walls. The song turns this upside down: the height falls, and the poor walk over it.
str: vv. 1–2: the strong city and its open gates.
vv. 3–4: trust in the Lord, the rock.
vv. 5–6: the lofty city laid low; the poor walk on it.
kw: A city with strength, but its walls here are God's “victory” or salvation (v. 1). Its security does not come from stone.
To lean on someone and feel safe. The word appears in both v. 3 and v. 4: trust is the only foundation the poet recommends.
Ṣûr is a great mass of rock, the mountain refuge of the land. Moses calls God “the Rock” in his song (Deuteronomy 32:4).
vv: Open the gates, so that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in.
The gates are open, not shut. What qualifies a person to enter is faithfulness, not birth or strength. Psalm 118, today's psalm, sings the same: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (118:19).
Trust in the Lord forever, for in the Lord God you have an everlasting rock.
This is the centre of the reading and the bridge to the Gospel.
The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy.
God reverses the order of things, as Mary will sing: “He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:52).
ch: The Fathers and the liturgy read the rock as Christ, following St Paul: “the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The Lectionary puts this song beside the Gospel of the two houses for that reason. Advent asks whether our security rests on walls of our own or on him.

r.h: The house on the rock
set: These are the closing words of the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7). The reading leaves out vv. 22–23, on those who did great things in Jesus' name and yet never knew him. In the land of Israel a dry valley can turn in an hour into a violent stream after the winter rain. Everyone listening would know how the house on the sand ends.
str: v. 21: not saying, but doing the Father's will.
vv. 24–25: the wise builder: same storm, house stands.
vv. 26–27: the foolish builder: same storm, great fall.
kw: A correct confession and a solemn title. But Jesus says it is not enough to say the right words.
Sensible, practical, knowing what the moment needs. The same word describes the wise bridesmaids (25:2). Its opposite is mōros, foolish.
The house “had been founded on rock” (v. 25). What matters happens before the storm, in the digging that no one sees.
vv: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.
Jesus speaks here with an astonishing authority: he himself is the “Lord” of the last day. And he points beyond himself to “my Father”.
Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
“These words of mine” take the place that the words of the Law hold in Israel's life. St James says the same: “be doers of the word, and not merely hearers” (James 1:22).
The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on rock.
The rain falls on both houses. Faith is not a promise of no storms. The difference appears only when the weather comes.
ch: The Catechism teaches from v. 21 that prayer means disposing the heart to do the Father's will (CCC 2611), and that one enters the Kingdom not by speaking words but by doing that will (CCC 2826). St Augustine closes his commentary on the Sermon on the Mount with these two houses: to hear and not to do is to build without a foundation (in substance).

qa: Does this Gospel mean that we are saved by works and not by faith?

No. Jesus does not set faith against action; he sets empty words against a real life. St Paul speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Grace comes first and is a gift, and it builds the house; the doing is what faith looks like when it is alive.
rite: St Francis Xavier (1506–1552) was one of the first companions of St Ignatius of Loyola. He landed in Goa in 1542 and preached among the fishing people of the Fishery Coast and in Travancore, before going on to Malacca, the Moluccas and Japan. He died on the island of Shangchuan, off the coast of China, and his body lies in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa. The Church honours him, with St Thérèse of Lisieux, as patron of the missions. He is a witness of today's Gospel for the Latin Catholics of India: a man who heard the words and acted on them.
study: If a storm came tomorrow, what in my life would stand? What would I find is built on sand?
St Francis Xavier gave up a promising career at the University of Paris to go to the ends of the known world. What word of Christ am I hearing without yet acting on it?

lead: Isaiah promises a day when the deaf will hear and the blind will see. In Matthew two blind men follow Jesus through the street, calling him Son of David, and he asks them one question: “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” The promise of the first reading meets a person in the second, and what it asks of the blind men is faith.

r.h: The eyes of the blind shall see
set: Earlier in this chapter Isaiah has been severe. He told Jerusalem's leaders that they were blinded and that the prophetic word was to them like a sealed scroll (29:9–12), and that they honoured God with their lips while their hearts were far from him (29:13). Today's verses answer that darkness with a promise of reversal.
str: v. 17: the land transformed: Lebanon and the fruitful field.
vv. 18–19: the deaf hear, the blind see, the poor rejoice.
vv. 20–21: the tyrant and the corrupt courts removed.
vv. 22–24: Jacob no longer ashamed; a people who sanctify God's name and learn.
kw: The poor and lowly who have no one to rely on but God. The word stands behind “Blessed are the meek” (Matthew 5:5).
Isaiah's favourite title for God is “the Holy One of Israel”. Holiness is the reason for joy here, and it comes down to the poor.
To buy back or set at liberty. “The Lord, who redeemed Abraham” (v. 22) goes back to the very beginning of God's choosing.
vv: On that day the deaf shall hear the words of a scroll, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see.
The “scroll” picks up the sealed book of v. 11, which no one could read. Now even the deaf hear it. Isaiah is speaking of both the body and the understanding.
The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord, and the neediest people shall exult in the Holy One of Israel.
Joy begins at the bottom of society. In the next verses the people who cheated them in the courts disappear.
And those who err in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction.
The end of the reading is a quiet miracle: minds and hearts healed. Opening the eyes is the easier part.
ch: When John the Baptist's messengers ask who he is, Jesus answers with Isaiah's signs: “the blind receive their sight” (Matthew 11:5). The Church reads these promises as fulfilled in him. His healings are messianic signs (CCC 549), and he opens the eyes of faith as well as the eyes of the body. Baptism came to be called “enlightenment” in the early Church (CCC 1216).

r.h: According to your faith
set: Matthew 8–9 gathers ten deeds of power after the Sermon on the Mount. This story comes near the end of the series, just after the raising of the ruler's daughter. Soon Jesus will reply to John: “the blind receive their sight” (11:5). Matthew has a similar story later, again of two blind men, near Jericho (20:29–34).
str: v. 27: the cry in the street.
v. 28: the question inside the house.
vv. 29–30a: the touch and the healing.
vv. 30b–31: the stern order, and the disobedience.
kw: The same cry as Kyrie eleison at Mass. It asks for God's covenant kindness, and it comes from people with nothing to offer.
Matthew's Gospel opens with this title (1:1), but here for the first time in the Gospel someone calls Jesus by it to his face. Blind men see what the learned do not.
Here it is trust in a person: “Do you believe that I am able?” The reply “Yes, Lord” is a whole creed in two words.
vv: As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying loudly, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”
How do blind men follow? By the sound of his voice and the crowd. That in itself is a picture of faith.
When he entered the house, the blind men came to him; and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.”
Jesus does not stop in the street. He lets them come further, into the house, and he draws their trust into words.
Then he touched their eyes and said, “According to your faith let it be done to you.”
This does not mean that faith itself is the power. The power is his touch; faith is the open door.
ch: The Catechism teaches that this cry of the blind men, “Have mercy on us, Son of David”, is renewed in the traditional prayer known as the Jesus Prayer, and that Jesus hears the prayer of faith (CCC 2616). The signs of Jesus attest that the Father has sent him, and they invite belief in him (CCC 548). In an Advent liturgy, the cry “Lord, have mercy” at the start of Mass stands in the same line.

qa: Why does Jesus tell them to keep silent, when he has healed them?

Matthew's phrase is strong: he “sternly ordered them” (9:30). “Son of David” could be heard as a political title, and Jesus would not be proclaimed in that sense. The Catechism says he accepted the title of Messiah with some reserve for this reason (CCC 439). His kingship would be shown fully only on the Cross. The two men's joy is easy to understand, but their disobedience is still disobedience.
study: Jesus asks, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” What is the “this” in my life just now, and how would I answer him?
Isaiah says those who grumble will accept instruction. Where am I grumbling, and what might God be trying to teach me?

lead: Isaiah promises a people in Zion that God will answer their cry, teach them, send rain and bind up their wounds. In Matthew that God has come to walk among the towns: Jesus sees the crowds, is moved with compassion, and sends out twelve men to do what he has been doing. The Lord who heals calls others to share the work.

r.h: This is the way; walk in it
set: Chapter 30 begins with a “woe” against those who sent to Egypt for help instead of trusting the Lord, probably in the time of King Hezekiah, when Assyria threatened Judah. The people refused to listen: “In returning and rest you shall be saved” (30:15). They would not. Yet God waits “to be gracious to you” (30:18), and today's promise follows from that. The reading omits v. 22, on throwing away idols.
str: v. 19: no more weeping; God hears.
vv. 20–21: bread of adversity, but the Teacher is seen and heard.
vv. 23–25: rain, grain, pastures, streams.
v. 26: light multiplied on the day of healing.
kw: To show kindness that is not owed. The verb appears in v. 18 and v. 19: God longs to do it.
From the same root as Torah, “instruction”. The people have refused the prophets (30:9–11). Now the Teacher himself will no longer hide.
The great biblical word for how one lives. “This is the way” is said from behind, as a parent speaks to a child learning to walk.
vv: Truly, O people in Zion, inhabitants of Jerusalem, you shall weep no more. He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry
God answers before the people have put their cry into words. The first thing he hears is the sound itself.
And when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left, your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, “This is the way; walk in it.”
The trials of v. 20 do not vanish, but the people are no longer alone in them.
on the day when the Lord binds up the injuries of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow.
The same hand that struck now binds up. Isaiah does not explain the mystery, but he ends with God as the doctor of his people.
ch: The Church hears “your Teacher” fulfilled in Christ, who says, “you have one teacher” (Matthew 23:8), and sits teaching on the mountain. The Bread and the Teacher come together in the Mass: the table of the word and the table of the Eucharist (Dei Verbum 21). The binding up of wounds is taken up in the Gospel of the day, where Jesus cures “every disease and every sickness”.

r.h: The harvest is plentiful
set: V. 35 almost repeats 4:23, and the two verses frame everything between them: the words of chapters 5–7 and the deeds of chapters 8–9. Now Matthew turns to the mission of the Twelve in chapter 10, the second great discourse of his Gospel. The reading leaves out the list of names (10:2–4).
str: 9:35: Jesus' work summed up: teaching, proclaiming, curing.
9:36: he sees the crowds and is moved.
9:37–38: the harvest and the prayer for laborers.
10:1: the Twelve receive authority.
10:5a, 6–8: they are sent: to Israel first, with his own message and works.
kw: Literally, to be moved in the bowels, the depths of a person. Mission begins here, in the heart of Jesus.
In the prophets the harvest is an image of God's final gathering (Joel 3:13; Isaiah 27:12). The last days have begun.
As a gift, at no cost. The same word comes in Romans 3:24: we are justified “by his grace as a gift”.
vv: When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
The image goes back to Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34. God promised to shepherd them himself.
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few
Jesus does not say, “The harvest is hopeless.” Those who look at people with his eyes see a harvest. The first response he asks for is not organisation but prayer (9:38).
You received without payment; give without payment.
The Twelve are told to do what Jesus has just done: cure the sick, raise the dead, cast out demons. Nothing is theirs by right, so nothing is for sale.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ's compassion toward the sick is a sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503), and that he associates his disciples with his own ministry of compassion and healing (CCC 1506). St Gregory the Great, preaching on the same saying in Luke, lamented that the world is full of priests, and yet few workers are found in God's harvest (in substance). Pope St Paul VI wrote that the Church “exists in order to evangelize” (Evangelii Nuntiandi 14).

qa: Why does Jesus say, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles”?

The Lectionary leaves out these words (v. 5b), but the question is a natural one. Jesus respects the order of God's plan: the promises were first made to Israel. So he says, “go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6). After the Resurrection the same Lord sends them to “all nations” (Matthew 28:19). The Catechism says the Kingdom was first announced to the children of Israel, and is meant for all people (CCC 543).
study: Jesus looked at the crowds and saw a harvest. When I look at my parish and my neighbourhood, what do I see?
“You received without payment.” What have I received from God that I could give away this week?

lead: This Sunday all four readings speak about a road. In Isaiah a voice calls for a highway in the desert, so that God may lead his exiled people home. The psalm says that righteousness will go before the Lord and “make a path for his steps”. Second Peter explains why the road seems so long: God's delay is his patience. Mark opens his Gospel with the same voice from Isaiah, now in the mouth of John the Baptist at the Jordan. The key words are comfort, way and repentance. God is on his way to us, and the road he asks us to level runs through our own hearts.

r.h: Comfort, O comfort my people
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah, often called the Book of Consolation, speak to the Jews in exile in Babylon, in the years before Cyrus of Persia took the city (539 BC) and allowed them to go home. Jerusalem and its Temple had been destroyed in 587 BC, and a generation had grown up in a foreign land. These chapters are generally attributed to a later prophet in the tradition of Isaiah, and the Church receives them as part of the one inspired book.

Today's verses are the opening of that message. It seems that the prophet overhears God's heavenly council giving orders: speak, cry out, build, climb. The Lectionary omits vv. 6–8, on the grass that withers and the word that stands forever.
str: vv. 1–2: God's command to comfort: the term is served.
vv. 3–5: a voice: prepare a highway in the desert; all people shall see God's glory.
vv. 9–11: Zion, the herald, announces: “Here is your God!” He comes with might, and he comes as a shepherd.
¶ The movement goes from God's word, to a road, to God's arrival. Exile ends not when the people have found the way back but when God comes to lead them.
kw: An imperative plural, said twice for urgency. Someone is being commanded to bring comfort: God sends messengers. Comfort here is not soothing words but the end of the sentence.

Literally “speak to the heart”. The phrase is used when Joseph reassures his frightened brothers (Genesis 50:21) and when God woos Israel in the desert (Hosea 2:14). God speaks to Jerusalem as to a beloved who has been far from home.
A feminine form: Zion herself is the messenger. The verb lies behind the Greek words for “to preach the good news”, and so behind Mark's euangelion today.
vv: Comfort, O comfort my people, says your God.
“My people” and “your God” are the words of the covenant. After the exile the relationship still stands.
A voice cries out: “In the wilderness prepare the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.

In the Hebrew, the wilderness is where the road is to be built. The Greek Old Testament joins the words differently, “the voice of one crying out in the wilderness”, and that is how Mark quotes it. Babylon was famous for its Processional Way for the god Marduk. Isaiah imagines a far greater road, across the desert, for the living God.
Then the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all people shall see it together
The return from exile is more than a local event. In the Hebrew the phrase is “all flesh”: the whole human race is the audience.

Get you up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good tidings; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good tidings, lift it up, do not fear; say to the cities of Judah, “Here is your God!”
Zion, who sat in mourning, now climbs and shouts. The whole Advent message fits into four words: Here is your God.
He will feed his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms, and carry them in his bosom, and gently lead the mother sheep.
The arm that “rules” in v. 10 is the same arm that carries the lambs in v. 11. Power and tenderness are one in God. Jesus takes up this image for himself (John 10:11).
ch: All four Gospels apply Isaiah 40:3 to John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4; John 1:23). Origen, preaching on Luke, says that this road is to be prepared within the human heart, which is wide enough to receive the Word of God (in substance). The Catechism teaches that when the Church celebrates the liturgy of Advent she makes present the ancient expectation of the Messiah (CCC 524). And Isaiah's “Comfort” is heard again wherever a broken life is told that its term is over, as in the sacrament of Penance.

r.h: Steadfast love and faithfulness will meet
set: Psalm 85 is a prayer of a people who have been brought back but are not yet whole. The opening verses remember that God “restored the fortunes of Jacob”; the middle asks “Will you be angry with us forever?” Many scholars place it after the return from exile, when the land was poor and the rebuilding slow, which is exactly the situation Isaiah's joyful promise left open. The Lectionary keeps only the last part, God's answer. The verses here follow the numbering of the Lectionary, one higher than the NRSV.
str: vv. 9–10: the psalmist listens: God speaks peace; salvation is near.
vv. 11–12: four virtues meet like persons; earth and heaven answer each other.
vv. 13–14: the land gives its fruit; righteousness goes before the Lord.
kw: God's faithful covenant kindness, the love that does not walk away.
What is solid and reliable. Ḥesed and ’ĕmet are often a pair, as in God's own name in Exodus 34:6 (CCC 214).
Right relations: with God, neighbour and land. In this psalm it is almost a herald who goes before the King.
Wholeness and well-being in every part of life, far more than the absence of war.
vv: Let me hear what God the Lord will speak, for he will speak peace to his people
The first act of the listening community is silence. The whole psalm hangs on someone waiting to hear.
Steadfast love and faithfulness will meet; righteousness and peace will kiss each other.
These are qualities, but the poet makes them meet like friends on a road. What sin keeps apart, God brings together.
Faithfulness will spring up from the ground, and righteousness will look down from the sky.
Heaven and earth meet. The Latin reads “truth has sprung from the earth” (veritas de terra orta est), and this verse came to be heard as a Christmas prophecy.
Righteousness will go before him, and will make a path for his steps.
The psalm ends on the theme of the day. The road in the desert appears again, and righteousness itself goes ahead like a herald.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this psalm, took “truth has sprung from the earth” as Christ born of a woman (in substance). St Bernard of Clairvaux, in a sermon for the Annunciation, imagined these four virtues as sisters who argue over fallen humanity and are reconciled in the coming of the Son (in substance). In the Mass today the psalm is the people's reply: “Lord, let us see your kindness, and grant us your salvation.”

r.h: The Lord is patient
set: This letter comes in the name of Simon Peter. Many scholars think that it was written later than the Apostle's lifetime, in his name and to guard his teaching. The Church received it as inspired Scripture. Its readers were being troubled by scoffers who asked, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (3:4). By then the first generation of Christians had died and the Lord had not returned. The reading gives the Church's answer to that disappointment.
str: v. 8: God's time is not ours.
v. 9: the delay is mercy.
v. 10: the day will come suddenly.
vv. 11–12: so how should we live? Waiting and hastening.
vv. 13–14: new heavens and a new earth; be found at peace.
kw: Literally “to be long of spirit”. It is the opposite of a short temper. The word describes God's way with a sinner.
“Hastening the coming of the day of God” (v. 12). A daring idea: the holy lives and repentance of believers are somehow part of God's timing (compare Acts 3:19–20).
Words from the world of sacrifice. The same pair of ideas describes Christ, “a lamb without defect or blemish” (1 Peter 1:19). What the Lamb is, the Church is called to become.
vv: with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like one day.
An echo of Psalm 90:4. The saying is not a code for calculating dates; it is the reason why we cannot calculate them.
The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some think of slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance.
This verse changes the question. We ask why God is late. Peter says that the time between is a gift, and that we are the ones being waited for.
But the day of the Lord will come like a thief

The image is from Jesus himself (Matthew 24:43). A note on the text. At the end of this verse the manuscripts differ. Some of the oldest Greek manuscripts read that the earth and its works “will be found”, and the NRSV renders this “disclosed”: everything will stand uncovered before God. Other manuscripts and the Vulgate read “will be burned up”, which the Malayalam POC follows. The first says that nothing can hide; the second that nothing will last. Both serve the letter's point.
But, in accordance with his promise, we wait for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.
The promise goes back to Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. The goal is a home, not an escape. Righteousness, restless in this world, at last finds a place to live.
Therefore, beloved, while you are waiting for these things, strive to be found by him at peace, without spot or blemish
Christian waiting is active. The fruit of the day of the Lord, peace, is meant to appear already in those who wait for it.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 9 when it teaches that God predestines no one to hell, and that the Church prays that all should come to repentance (CCC 1037). It takes “new heavens and a new earth” (v. 13) as the Scripture's name for the mysterious renewal of the universe (CCC 1043), and says that the message of the Last Judgment calls us to conversion while God still gives us time (CCC 1041). St Cyril of Jerusalem taught his catechumens that we preach not only one coming of Christ but a second, far more glorious than the first (in substance). That is the double vision of Advent.

r.h: The beginning of the good news
set: Mark is generally thought to be the earliest of the four Gospels. Tradition links him with St Peter's preaching at Rome. He has no story of the birth of Jesus. He begins with John in the wilderness, because that is where the Good News begins to be heard. Mark's Gospel is the Sunday Gospel of this new liturgical year, Year B.

The desert east of Jerusalem, running down to the Jordan, is a place heavy with memory. Israel came through the wilderness and crossed the Jordan into the land. A Jewish community at Qumran, not far from the same river, took Isaiah 40:3 as its own charter for living in the desert (Rule of the Community 8). Coming out to John meant going back to the beginning.
str: v. 1: the title of the book.
vv. 2–3: the prophetic word: messenger and voice.
vv. 4–5: John's preaching and the crowds.
v. 6: John's clothing and food.
vv. 7–8: John points away from himself.
kw: The first word of the Gospel, and the first word of Genesis in the Greek Old Testament (en archē) and of John's Gospel. Something is being created anew.
In the Roman world the word could be used for the news of an emperor's birth or victory. Isaiah's herald (40:9) stands behind it in the Greek Bible. Mark's news is about a different king.
A change of mind and direction. Behind it stands the Hebrew idea of turning back (šûb). Levelling the road means this: repentance is the road-building of the Gospel.
John knows that he is not the strong one. His whole ministry is a pointing finger.
vv: The beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

A note on the text. A few important early manuscripts lack “the Son of God”, while most have it. It is generally kept. Either way, the Gospel's structure confirms it: the voice at the Baptism says “You are my Son” (1:11), and at the Cross a Roman centurion says “Truly this man was God’s Son!” (15:39).
As it is written in the prophet Isaiah, “See, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way;
The first line comes from Malachi 3:1 (with an echo of Exodus 23:20), the second from Isaiah 40:3. Mark names the greater prophet for both. Later copyists, puzzled, changed it to “in the prophets”.
John the baptizer appeared in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
Jewish practice knew ritual washings that were repeated. John's baptism seems to have been a single act of turning back to God. It pointed forward; it did not yet have the power of Christian Baptism.
Now John was clothed with camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.

This is what Elijah wore (2 Kings 1:8), and Malachi promised that Elijah would return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). Locusts were permitted food (Leviticus 11:22). He eats what the wilderness gives.
I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the thong of his sandals.
A later rabbinic saying holds that a disciple should do for his teacher everything a slave does, except untie his sandals (in substance). John says he is not worthy even of that.
I have baptized you with water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.
The prophets promised the outpouring of the Spirit in the last days (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28). Water can only wash; the Spirit makes new.
ch: The Catechism calls John “the Lord's immediate precursor or forerunner, sent to prepare his way” (CCC 523), the Elijah who must come (CCC 718). It recalls that his baptism of repentance was the setting where the public life of Jesus began (CCC 535). St Augustine, in a sermon on the Baptist, contrasts John as the voice with Christ as the Word: the voice sounds for a moment and passes, and the Word remains (in substance). This is the humility of every preacher, catechist and parent: to be a voice for someone greater.

qa: Why does Mark say “in the prophet Isaiah” when part of the quotation is from Malachi?

This was a known way of citing: a combined quotation could be attributed to the more important prophet. Mark's real interest is in Isaiah, the prophet of the road through the desert and the coming of God. Some later manuscripts changed the wording to “in the prophets” to remove the difficulty, which is good evidence that “Isaiah” is the original.
Why does Mark have no Christmas story?

He is not denying it; he begins where the Apostles' own preaching began, with John's baptism (see Acts 1:22; 10:37). Matthew and Luke add the infancy stories, and John goes back further still, to the eternal Word. The four Gospels together give the Church the full portrait.
Will the world really be burned up, as 2 Peter says?

Fire is the Bible's language for God's judgment and purification. The Church teaches that the visible universe is destined to be transformed, not simply thrown away (CCC 1047), and that we do not know how this will be (CCC 1048; Gaudium et Spes 39). Peter's own conclusion is about how we live now.
rite: In the Roman calendar Advent has two stages. Until 16 December its prayers look above all to Christ's second coming; from 17 December they prepare directly for Christmas. This is why the Sunday readings move from the end of time to John the Baptist, who appears on two Sundays of Advent. Year B, which began last Sunday, gives us Mark. On Tuesday the Church keeps the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary (CCC 490–493). The “spot or blemish” of today's second reading may remind us of it: God prepared one woman for his coming, and she was preserved from every stain of original sin from the first moment of her conception, by the merits of her Son.
study: Isaiah says, “speak to the heart”. Who around me needs a word of comfort from the Lord this week, and from whom do I need to receive it?
Psalm 85 says that love and truth, justice and peace, will meet. In which of my relationships are they still apart?
2 Peter tells us that God's delay is patience with us. What is he patiently waiting for in me?
John says, “The one who is more powerful than I is coming.” In my service to others, do I point to Christ or to myself?

lead: Isaiah sings of a desert that blooms, of the blind and the lame healed, and of a holy road home. In Luke the song reaches a crowded house: friends open a roof, and Jesus, seeing their faith, forgives a paralysed man and then tells him to walk. Isaiah says, “He will come and save you”; the Gospel shows him doing it, and shows that the deepest wound he heals is sin.

r.h: The Holy Way
set: This chapter follows a dark vision of judgment on Edom (Isaiah 34), and its language is so close to chapters 40–55 that many scholars see it as closely related to them. It speaks of a road home through a desert transformed. Yesterday we heard the call to build the road (40:3). Today we see who walks on it.
str: vv. 1–2: the desert rejoices and blossoms.
vv. 3–4: strengthen the weak: “Here is your God.”
vv. 5–7: the blind, deaf, lame and mute healed; water in the desert.
vv. 8–10: the Holy Way; the ransomed return to Zion with singing.
kw: A spring flower of the dry lands. The exact plant is uncertain. It appears here and in the Song of Songs (2:1). The point is a colour no one expected in the waste.
No ordinary road: God has set it apart. It recalls the pilgrim roads to Zion, and it also becomes a name for life with God. The first Christians were called people of “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
The gō’ēl was the relative who paid to buy back a family member from debt or slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49). God acts here as the next of kin of his people.
vv: Say to those who are of a fearful heart, “Be strong, do not fear! Here is your God. He will come with vengeance, with terrible recompense. He will come and save you.”
“Vengeance” here means that God will set right what was done to his people. Its last word is “save”.
Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped
These are the very signs Jesus names for the disciples of John: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, … the deaf hear” (Matthew 11:5). Today's Gospel gives one of them.
And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
Sorrow and sighing are pictured as intruders who run away when the procession arrives. Everything sad has at last been made to leave.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' healings are messianic signs, which announce a far greater liberation: from the slavery of sin (CCC 549). The Church reads Isaiah 35 in Advent so that we may recognise him when he comes. The Holy Way is now open in Christ, who says, “I am the way” (John 14:6).

r.h: Friend, your sins are forgiven
set: This is the first time Pharisees appear in Luke, together with teachers of the law from Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem. They are serious, observant men, who have come to find out about a new teacher. The scene opens a series of five disputes (5:17–6:11). Luke is careful to note at the start: “the power of the Lord was with him to heal.”
str: v. 17: the audience and the power.
vv. 18–19: the friends and the roof.
v. 20: the surprise: sins forgiven.
vv. 21–24: the question and the answer.
vv. 25–26: the man walks; everyone glorifies God.
kw: Literally “man” or “O human being”, as the Malayalam POC keeps it. It is a plain and direct form of address.
Power that is rightfully held. Daniel 7:13–14 shows one like a Son of Man receiving authority from God. Jesus claims it “on earth”, here and now.
Literally things beyond expectation. We have the word “paradox” from it. “We have seen strange things today”: sēmeron, today, is a key word of Luke's Gospel (2:11; 4:21; 19:9; 23:43).
vv: When he saw their faith, he said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven you.”

“Their” faith: Jesus looks at the friends, and the man is healed because of what they did. This is the root of all intercession. Jesus does not say that the man's sickness was his punishment; he goes first to the deepest need.
Who is this who is speaking blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?
The question is correct, and their theology is sound: only God forgives sins. The only thing they have not yet seen is who is standing in front of them.
Immediately he stood up before them, took what he had been lying on, and went to his home, glorifying God.
The visible sign supports the invisible gift. The bed that carried him he now carries. He leaves by the door, and he and the crowd end up doing the same thing: glorifying God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that “only God forgives sins”, and that Jesus, as Son of God, exercises this divine power and gives it to men in his name (CCC 1441). It opens its teaching on the sacraments of healing with this very scene: Christ, physician of soul and body, who forgave the paralytic and restored him, willed that his Church continue this work (CCC 1421). St Ambrose, whose memorial is today, comments on this passage in his book on Luke: how great is the Lord, who forgives some for the merit of others (in substance).

qa: Did the man's paralysis come from his sins?

The text does not say so. Some in that time took sickness to be a punishment for sin, but Jesus rejects this as a general rule (John 9:2–3). He treats both needs because he is the healer of the whole person (CCC 1503). Sin, not paralysis, is the deeper bondage, and that is why it comes first.
rite: St Ambrose (died 397), governor at Milan and still a catechumen, was acclaimed bishop by the people, and was ordained on 7 December 374, the date of today's memorial. He preached so well that he helped bring St Augustine to the faith, and he baptised him at Easter in 387. He is one of the great Doctors of the Latin Church. He wrote the Advent hymn Veni, Redemptor gentium, and he spoke of Mary as a type of the Church (Lumen Gentium 63). His memorial stands just before tomorrow's Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception, and in a sense he prepares us to keep it: to look at Mary is to see what the Church is called to be.
study: Who has carried me to Jesus when I could not go myself? Whom could I carry by my prayer and my faith today?
When did I last hear the words “your sins are forgiven”? What keeps me from going to confession this Advent?

lead: In the middle of Advent the Church stops to look at the woman God prepared for the coming of his Son. Today’s solemnity is about Mary’s own beginning: from the first moment of her existence in the womb of her mother, she was kept from all stain of original sin, by a unique grace of God and because of the merits of Christ. It is not about the conception of Jesus, which is the Annunciation, though the Gospel read today is the Annunciation, because that is where Scripture shows us who Mary already is.

The readings go from a garden to a small town. In Genesis the first man and woman hide from God, and God speaks the first promise: there will be enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring. The psalm sings of the victory God has made known. Ephesians says that God chose us in Christ “before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless”. In Luke the angel greets a young woman in Nazareth as one already filled with grace, and she answers, “let it be with me according to your word.” The key words are enmity, chosen and grace.

r.h: Where are you?
set: Genesis 2–3 tells of the beginning of sin in the language of a story: a garden, a tree, a serpent. The Catechism says that this account “uses figurative language, but affirms a primeval event” (CCC 390). Our reading begins just after the man and the woman have eaten and have hidden among the trees (3:8). Trust in God has broken, and now fear and shame enter.

The Lectionary leaps from v. 15 to v. 20. It leaves out the consequences for the woman and the man (vv. 16–19) and keeps the promise and the name of Eve, so that the first mother of the living stands beside the promise.
str: vv. 9–13: God’s questions: Where are you? Who told you? What have you done? Each person passes the blame to another.
vv. 14–15: God’s word to the serpent: a curse, and a lasting enmity with the woman and her offspring.
v. 20: the man names his wife Eve, “the mother of all living”.
¶ God asks the man and the woman questions, but he does not question the serpent. He simply pronounces sentence, and inside that sentence is the first hope of the human race.
kw: A word for deep and lasting hostility. It is God who puts it there: “I will put”. The serpent’s friendship with the human race is not allowed to stand.
A collective word that can also point to one descendant. The promise looks down the generations, and Christian reading sees it reach its goal in Christ.
The same Hebrew verb is used for both blows: he will strike your head, you will strike his heel. The blows are not equal: one is to the head, the other to the heel.
The name sounds like the Hebrew word for living, ḥay. After the sentence of death, the man gives his wife a name of life.
vv: But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
God knows the answer. The question is an invitation to come out of hiding. It is the first question God asks in the Bible, and he is still asking it.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.

A note on the text. The Hebrew says “he” (hû’) will strike, and so do the Greek Old Testament, the NRSV and the POC. The Latin Vulgate tradition reads “she” (ipsa), which is why Western art so often shows Mary with the serpent under her foot. Both point to the same victory: the Son wins it, and his mother shares in it by his grace.
The man named his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
The Fathers set Eve and Mary side by side. Comparing the two, they call Mary “the Mother of the living” (CCC 494).
ch: The Church calls Genesis 3:15 the Protoevangelium, the “first Gospel”, the first announcement of the Messiah and of a battle between the serpent and the Woman (CCC 410). Many Fathers and Doctors see in this woman the mother of Christ, the “new Eve” (CCC 411). St Irenaeus wrote that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was untied by Mary’s obedience (quoted in CCC 494; Lumen Gentium 56). The last book of the Bible returns to the same scene, with “that ancient serpent” and a woman who gives birth to the Messiah (Revelation 12).

r.h: All the ends of the earth have seen
set: Psalm 98 is one of the hymns that celebrate the Lord as King (Psalms 93–99). It calls for a new song because God has acted, and it sees his saving deed in the sight of all nations. Its language is close to the second part of Isaiah.
str: v. 1: the call to sing, and the reason: God’s right hand has won.
vv. 2–3: God’s victory is made known, because he has remembered Israel.
v. 4: all the earth is invited to shout for joy.
kw: In the Psalms a new song answers a new act of God. Today the new thing is the beginning of the Redeemer’s coming.
From the same root as the name Jesus (Yēšûa‘). The NRSV says “victory”; the word also means rescue and salvation.
God’s faithful covenant love, which he “has remembered”. For God, to remember is to act.
vv: O sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things.
He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the victory of our God.
Israel first, then the whole earth. Mary’s own song says the same thing: God has helped Israel “in remembrance of his mercy” (Luke 1:54).
ch: The Church sings this psalm at the Mass of Christmas Day as well as today. The marvel that begins hidden in Mary’s life is shown to all the ends of the earth in her Son. On this solemnity the psalm also reminds us that the praise goes to God: what is celebrated in Mary is his work.

r.h: Chosen before the foundation of the world
set: The letter comes to us under Paul’s name and speaks from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple carrying on his teaching, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself. After the greeting it opens with a great blessing, on the Jewish model of “Blessed be God”, which runs from v. 3 to v. 14. In the Greek this is a single long sentence.
str: v. 3: blessing God who has blessed us in Christ.
vv. 4–6: he chose us before creation, to be holy and to be his adopted children.
vv. 11–12: in Christ we too have received an inheritance, to live for the praise of his glory.
kw: God’s choice comes before anything we do. It is made “in Christ”, the phrase that returns again and again in this passage.
The word used in the Greek Old Testament for a sacrificial animal without defect. The letter uses the same pair of words for the Church, “holy and without blemish” (5:27).

From the verb charitoō, to fill with grace, to favour. In the New Testament this verb appears only here and in Luke 1:28, in the angel’s greeting to Mary. Today’s two readings are joined by this one rare word.
vv: just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
The goal is not only a clean record but love, “before him”. The Catechism applies this verse directly to Mary (CCC 492). What God wills for all of us, he gave to her from the first moment.
He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will,
Adoption (huiothesia) was a legal act in the Roman world that gave a full place in the family. All of this comes “through Jesus Christ”, and Mary is no exception: she too is saved through her Son.
to the praise of his glorious grace that he freely bestowed on us in the Beloved.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Father blessed Mary more than any other created person “in Christ with every spiritual blessing”, and chose her “in Christ before the foundation of the world” (CCC 492, quoting this passage). The Church looks at Mary and sees what she herself hopes to become: in the Blessed Virgin the Church has already reached the perfection by which she exists without spot or wrinkle, while the rest of us still strive to grow in holiness (CCC 829; Lumen Gentium 65).

r.h: Greetings, favored one
set: Luke has just told of the angel’s visit to Zechariah in the Temple at Jerusalem, a priest in the sanctuary, who doubts (1:5–25). Now the same angel goes to a village never named in the Old Testament, to a young woman who is engaged and not yet living with her husband. The contrast is deliberate.

Betrothal among the Jews of that time was a binding bond, already close to marriage, which came before the bride moved to her husband’s house. So Joseph, a descendant of David, is legally the one through whom Jesus belongs to the house of David.
str: vv. 26–27: the time, the place, the persons.
vv. 28–29: the greeting, and Mary’s perplexity.
vv. 30–33: the first message: a son, Jesus, the heir of David.
v. 34: Mary’s question.
vv. 35–37: the second message: the Holy Spirit, the Son of God, the sign of Elizabeth.
v. 38: Mary’s answer.
kw: The usual Greek greeting, but it literally means “rejoice”. Many commentators hear in it the prophets’ call to the daughter of Zion to rejoice because the Lord is in her midst (Zephaniah 3:14–15; Zechariah 9:9).

A perfect passive participle of charitoō: one who has been graced and remains so. The angel uses it in place of her name, as if it were her title. The Latin gratia plena and the POC “ദൈവകൃപ നിറഞ്ഞവളേ” bring this out. The grammar alone does not prove the dogma, but the Church has come to see in this word the depth of what God had already done in her (CCC 490–491).

The word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud settling on the tent of meeting when God’s glory filled it (Exodus 40:35). Mary is the new dwelling of God. The same verb returns in the cloud of the Transfiguration (Luke 9:34).
The feminine of the word for slave or servant, a title of honour for those who belong to God. She uses it again in her song (1:48).
vv: And he came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.”

“The Lord is with you” is what God says to those he calls to a great task, like Moses and Gideon (Exodus 3:12; Judges 6:12). Here it comes with no word of Mary’s achievement. Everything begins from grace.
Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?”
Literally, “since I do not know a man”, which is how the POC renders it. This is not the doubt of Zechariah. She does not ask for a sign but asks how it will happen.
The angel said to her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God.
This is the conception of Jesus, by the Holy Spirit. Today’s feast celebrates something earlier: the grace that made Mary ready to receive him.
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
The Greek verb genoito expresses a wish, a glad desire. Grace has not removed her freedom; it has made her able to say a whole yes.
ch: Pope Pius IX, in the bull Ineffabilis Deus (1854), defined that Mary, from the first instant of her conception, by a singular grace of God and in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, was preserved from all stain of original sin (CCC 491). Holding on to God’s word with her whole heart, and with no sin to hold her back, she gave herself entirely to the person and work of her Son (CCC 494). St Bernard, preaching on this passage, pictures the whole world waiting for her answer (in substance). St Augustine says that Mary was more blessed for receiving Christ by faith than for conceiving him in the flesh (in substance; CCC 506).

qa: Is the Immaculate Conception the same as the Virgin Birth?

No, though the two are often confused. The Immaculate Conception concerns Mary’s own beginning in the womb of her mother, whom tradition names Anne: she was preserved from original sin. The virginal conception concerns Jesus: he was conceived in Mary by the Holy Spirit, without a human father (CCC 496–498).
If Mary was without sin, did she need a Saviour?

Yes, and she says so: “my spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (Luke 1:47). She was redeemed “in a more exalted fashion” by the merits of her Son (CCC 492). St Bernard and St Thomas Aquinas had difficulty with the doctrine for this very reason. Blessed John Duns Scotus helped the Church to see that keeping someone from falling is a more perfect rescue than lifting her up after a fall (in substance).
Where is this in the Bible?

Scripture does not state the doctrine in so many words. Ineffabilis Deus points to Genesis 3:15 and Luke 1:28, read within the faith of the Church across the centuries. The Fathers called Mary all-holy (Panagia) (CCC 493), and the Church’s understanding grew until it was solemnly defined.
rite: In the Roman Rite this is a solemnity, with white vestments in the middle of violet Advent. The universal law of the Latin Church lists it among the holy days of obligation (Code of Canon Law, can. 1246), though bishops’ conferences may adjust this, so follow the direction of your own diocese. The Collect of the Mass says it all: God prepared a worthy dwelling for his Son and preserved Mary from every stain by virtue of the Death of his Son, which he foresaw (in substance). Four years after the definition, at Lourdes in 1858, the Lady told St Bernadette, “I am the Immaculate Conception.” The doctrine does not rest on that private revelation. In Advent the solemnity teaches us how to wait: God prepares the place where his Son will come.
study: God’s first question is “Where are you?” Where am I hiding from him at present, and what would it mean to answer him?
Ephesians 1:4 says that God chose me “to be holy and blameless before him in love”. How does it change my day to believe that holiness is God’s plan for me and not only my own effort?
Mary’s sinlessness did not make her life easy or remove her freedom. What does her “let it be” teach me about my own freedom?
How can I explain to someone, simply and correctly, the difference between the Immaculate Conception and the virginal conception of Jesus?

lead: Two voices speak to tired people today. Isaiah tells the exiles that the God who calls the stars by name never grows weary and gives his strength to the faint. In the Gospel Jesus says, “Come to me, all you that are weary”. The psalm, “Bless the Lord, O my soul”, gives thanks for the God who forgives and heals. What the prophet promised, Jesus now offers in person.

r.h: He does not faint or grow weary
set: Isaiah 40–55, the Book of Consolation, speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon in the years before Cyrus let them go home (539 BC). They are surrounded by great temples and by the worship of the stars, and they feel forgotten. This passage answers their complaint.
str: vv. 25–26: God has no equal; he brings out the stars like an army and calls each by name.
v. 27: Israel’s complaint.
vv. 28–31: God never tires, and he gives strength to those who wait for him.
kw: God’s otherness: nothing in creation can be compared with him. Yet in v. 29 the Holy One bends down to the faint.
To wait with eager hope. The POC translates “those who trust in God”, which brings out the same attitude from another side.
vv: Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, “My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God”?
God takes up the people’s complaint in their own words before he answers it. An honest complaint is a beginning of prayer.
He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless.
but those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.
The line goes from flying to running to walking. The strength of God is given most of all for the long and ordinary walk.
ch: The Catechism says that hope responds to the longing for happiness God has put in every heart, and keeps us from discouragement (CCC 1818). The Church reads these chapters throughout Advent because the people still waiting are ourselves. The God who brought the exiles home is the God who comes to us in his Son.

r.h: Come to me
set: These three verses are found only in Matthew. Jesus has just spoken of unbelieving towns and has thanked the Father for revealing himself to “infants” (11:20–27). Now he turns to all who are worn out. The words sound like the invitation to Wisdom in Sirach 51:23–27, where the teacher calls people to come near and to put their necks under her yoke.
str: v. 28: the invitation and the promise of rest.
v. 29: take my yoke, learn from me.
v. 30: the reason: my yoke is easy.
kw: The wooden frame that joins oxen for work. Jewish teachers spoke of the yoke of the Law. Jesus does not offer an idle life. He offers a yoke, but it is his.
The same word as “the meek” of the Beatitudes (5:5). The one who teaches has the same gentle heart he asks of us.
It also means kind, good, well suited. A well-made yoke fits the ox and does not gall it.
vv: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
The “all” has no conditions. The rest he promises is anapausis, refreshment, and it is a gift from him: “I will give”.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
“Rest for your souls” echoes Jeremiah 6:16. A disciple (mathētēs) is one who learns, and here the lesson is Jesus’ own heart.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
ch: The Catechism quotes “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me” when it teaches that the Word became flesh to be our model of holiness (CCC 459). Matthew’s readers would hear that Jesus speaks as God’s Wisdom in person. What Advent promises is not only that God will lift our burden, but that he will walk under it with us.

qa: How can Jesus call his yoke easy, when he also tells us to take up the cross?
The demand is real (16:24). The difference is that we do not carry it alone or by our own strength. Love makes heavy things bearable, and he is the one who walks beside us.
study: Isaiah 40:27 gives the people’s complaint in their own words. What would my own complaint to God sound like today?
What burden am I carrying alone that I could bring to Jesus at Mass today?

lead: “Do not fear”, God says three times in this chapter of Isaiah to a people who feel as small as a worm, and he promises to turn the desert into a garden. The psalm praises the Lord who is good to all. In the Gospel Jesus names John the Baptist as the greatest of those born of women, and as the Elijah who was to come. God’s great work begins from what looks small and dry, and the kingdom now stands at the door.

r.h: I will help you
set: The exiles in Babylon have lost their land, their king and their Temple. In this chapter God is speaking of the conqueror he is raising up from the east (41:2), who would later be named as Cyrus. He turns to tell Israel, his servant, not to be afraid. Our passage has two parts: a promise to the helpless and a picture of a new Exodus.
str: vv. 13–14: God holds Israel’s hand: Do not fear.
vv. 15–16: the helpless one becomes a threshing sledge.
vv. 17–20: God gives water and trees in the desert, so that all may know his hand.
kw: The next of kin, who by law had to buy back a relative from slavery or debt (Leviticus 25; Ruth 4). God makes himself Israel’s closest relative.
A picture of how small and despised the exiles felt. God does not deny their weakness; he speaks tenderly to it.
Isaiah’s favourite name for God. It joins two things that seem far apart: the God beyond all things and this one small people.
vv: For I, the Lord your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, “Do not fear, I will help you.”
Parents hold the hand of a small child like this. The same picture is used for Cyrus in 45:1, but there it is for a task; here it is for comfort.
Do not fear, you worm Jacob, you insect Israel! I will help you, says the Lord; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.
A note on the text. The Hebrew as it stands reads “men of Israel”, which the POC follows. “Insect” in the NRSV follows the Syriac version, which keeps the parallel with “worm”.
I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys; I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.
The journey home is pictured as a new Exodus, with water in the desert as at the rock (Exodus 17). Seven kinds of tree follow in v. 19, a whole forest where there was only sand.
ch: The Church hears in these verses the coming of the true Redeemer, the Son of God who became our next of kin by taking our flesh. The Catechism recalls that he came to give his life as a ransom for many (CCC 622). The water in the desert also points to the Spirit and to Baptism, the living water Christ promises (John 7:37–39).

r.h: No one greater than John
set: John is in Herod’s prison (11:2). He has sent his disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who is to come. After answering them, Jesus turns to the crowd and speaks about John, who stands at the turning point between the prophets and the kingdom.
str: v. 11: John is the greatest, yet the least in the kingdom is greater.
vv. 12–13: from John until now the kingdom suffers violence; the prophets and the law led up to him.
vv. 14–15: John is the Elijah who is to come. Let anyone with ears listen.
kw: A difficult word. It can be passive, “suffers violence”, as the NRSV and the POC take it, recalling what is happening to John and will happen to Jesus. Others take it as middle, the kingdom “forces its way”. Many spiritual writers read the verse of the strong effort needed to enter the kingdom.
Literally “smaller”. It does not compare holiness. John stands at the threshold, and those who enter the kingdom receive what he could only announce.
vv: Truly I tell you, among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist; yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
The point is the greatness of what has come, not a low view of John. It is a statement about the gift of the kingdom.
and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come.
Malachi 4:5–6 promised that Elijah would come before the day of the Lord. “If you are willing” shows that this cannot be proved: it is seen by those who accept it.
ch: The Catechism says that John surpasses all the prophets and is the last of them; he inaugurates the Gospel, already from his mother’s womb welcomes the coming of Christ, and rejoices as “the friend of the bridegroom” (CCC 523; see CCC 719). Each Advent the Church lets John prepare her again, so that she may recognise the one he points to.

study: God speaks tenderly to a “worm”. Where do I feel small and helpless, and can I hear “Do not fear” there?
What has the Lord already given me in the kingdom, by Baptism and the Eucharist, that I forget to be thankful for?

lead: Today’s readings share one sad note: what might have been. Through Isaiah God sighs over a people who would not listen: “O that you had paid attention to my commandments!” Psalm 1 sets the two ways side by side. In the Gospel Jesus compares his generation to sulking children who will not join any game. God is not hard to please; it is we who find reasons not to answer.

r.h: O that you had listened
set: Chapter 48 closes the first part of the Book of Consolation (Isaiah 40–48), which has been speaking of Cyrus and the fall of Babylon. Just after our passage comes the call “Go out from Babylon” (48:20). Before sending the people home, God looks back on why they were in exile.
str: v. 17: God’s self-introduction: Redeemer, Holy One, teacher, guide.
v. 18: the wish: if only you had listened.
v. 19: what they would have had: descendants like the sand, a name that lasts.
kw: Well-being in every part of life. The NRSV has “prosperity”, the POC has “peace”. Both are part of the word’s meaning.
The NRSV has “success”, the POC has “justice”. The word means being in right order with God and neighbour, and the good that comes from it.
vv: I am the Lord your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go.
God’s commandments are not a test to catch us out. They are the teaching of someone who wants our good.
O that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your prosperity would have been like a river, and your success like the waves of the sea;
This is the voice of disappointed love. The river never stops and the waves keep coming: that was the life God wanted to give.
your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains;
This recalls the promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). God’s promise has not been withdrawn: the very next verses send the people home.
ch: The Catechism calls the moral law the work of divine Wisdom, “fatherly instruction, God’s pedagogy”, which shows the ways that lead to the promised beatitude (CCC 1950). Isaiah’s God who “teaches you for your own good” is the same. In Advent these words are a call to examine our conscience before Christmas: not to despair over what might have been, but to listen today.

r.h: We played the flute
set: Jesus is still speaking about John the Baptist (11:7–19). He compares “this generation” to children in a marketplace, playing at weddings and funerals. Some children call out, and the others will not play either game. So people reject John as too severe and reject Jesus as too friendly.
str: vv. 16–17: the parable of the children.
vv. 18–19a: its application: John and the Son of Man are both refused.
v. 19b: yet wisdom is vindicated.
kw: Those of that time who refused to respond. Jesus’ words are not about a whole people: many in Israel followed him, and the warning is for every generation, ours too.
God’s saving plan. In Matthew 11 Jesus speaks and acts as God’s Wisdom.
vv: ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not mourn.’
Flute for a wedding, wailing for a funeral. John’s call to repentance is the dirge; Jesus’ meals with sinners are the wedding.
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon’;
the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.”

A note on the text. Some manuscripts read “by her children”, as in Luke 7:35. The reading “deeds” is the better attested in Matthew, and it recalls “the deeds of the Messiah” in 11:2. The insult “friend of tax collectors and sinners” is, without meaning to be, a true description of him.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus scandalised the Pharisees by eating with tax collectors and sinners as familiarly as with themselves (CCC 588). That table continues in the Eucharist. The passage warns us not to make God fit our own taste: he comes in the way he chooses, in the austere voice of John and in the warm welcome of Jesus.

qa: Is Jesus blaming the Jewish people here?

No. “This generation” means those who refused to answer him, and many of his own people did answer: all his first disciples were Jews. The Church firmly rejects any such blame (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). The words are addressed to us, who also find excuses.
study: What excuse do I use most often when God’s call comes in a form I do not like?
“O that you had paid attention”: what is one thing God has been asking me for a long time, which I could begin today?

lead: Earlier this week Jesus spoke of John as the Elijah who was to come. Today the Church goes back to Elijah himself, in the fiery words of Sirach, and then to Jesus’ answer on the way down from the mountain of the Transfiguration: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him.” The psalm prays, “let your face shine, that we may be saved.” Advent asks us whether we would recognise God’s messenger if he stood in front of us.

r.h: A prophet like fire
set: Jesus ben Sira was a Jewish teacher at Jerusalem around 180 BC, and his grandson later translated the book into Greek in Egypt. It is one of the deuterocanonical books, received by the Catholic Church as Scripture. Chapters 44–50 are a long “praise of famous men” which runs through Israel’s history. Elijah’s turn comes after a time of decline under the kings.
str: vv. 1–3: Elijah’s deeds: the word like a torch, the famine, the fire from heaven.
v. 4: “How glorious you were”.
v. 9: his being taken up (2 Kings 2:11).
v. 10: what is written of his return (Malachi 4:5–6).
v. 11: a blessing on those who see him.
kw: The picture that sums up Elijah: fire on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) and fire twice on the soldiers (2 Kings 1:10, 12), which make the “three times” of v. 3, and at the end a chariot of fire (2 Kings 2:11). His word itself burns.
The Greek of v. 10 speaks of God’s fixed time. Elijah’s return is part of God’s plan and not a chance event.
vv: Then Elijah arose, a prophet like fire, and his word burned like a torch.
At the appointed time, it is written, you are destined to calm the wrath of God before it breaks out in fury, to turn the hearts of parents to their children, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.
Sirach is drawing on Malachi. The angel uses the same words about John the Baptist: “to turn the hearts of parents to their children” (Luke 1:17).
Happy are those who saw you and were adorned with your love! For we also shall surely live.
A note on the text. This verse is damaged in the Hebrew and the versions differ. The NRSV says “we also shall surely live”; the POC says “they will live”. The hope is clear in either case.
ch: The Catechism says that John is “Elijah [who] must come”: the fire of the Spirit dwells in him and makes him the forerunner of the coming Lord (CCC 718). The East and West both honour Elijah as the model of the prophet on fire with zeal for God, and the Carmelite tradition looks to him as a father. Fire in Scripture also points to the Spirit who comes at Pentecost (Acts 2:3).

r.h: Elijah has already come
set: Peter, James and John have just seen Jesus transfigured, with Moses and Elijah beside him (17:1–8). Coming down, they ask the natural question: the scribes teach, from Malachi, that Elijah must come first. If the end is here, where is Elijah?
str: v. 9a: coming down the mountain.
v. 10: the disciples’ question.
vv. 11–12: Jesus’ answer: Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased.
v. 13: the disciples understand: he means John.
kw: The word used in the Greek of Malachi for Elijah’s work (Malachi 4:6 in the English Bible), close to Sirach’s “restore”. John’s call to repentance was the beginning of the restoration.
To know fully, to see who someone truly is. Those who saw only a strange preacher in the desert did not see the messenger of God.
vv: And the disciples asked him, “Why, then, do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
It is a fair question, and the scribes were reading the prophet correctly. What they lacked was the recognition of its fulfilment.
but I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but they did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands.”
Matthew has told how Herod Antipas had John killed (14:1–12). “They” here means those in power who rejected him, and not a people. The messenger’s fate foreshadows that of the Master.
Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them about John the Baptist.
ch: St Gregory the Great explains that John was Elijah in spirit and not in person (in substance), which is also how the angel puts it: “with the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17).
