The Church sees in John’s path the pattern of Christian witness: to prepare the way, to be rejected if necessary, and to point beyond oneself.

rite: Today many Latin Catholics keep the memory of Our Lady of Guadalupe. According to the tradition, in December 1531, on the hill of Tepeyac near what is now Mexico City, Mary appeared to St Juan Diego, an Indigenous convert, and spoke to him in his own language, Nahuatl. Her image on his cloak is still venerated in the basilica there. St John Paul II canonised Juan Diego in 2002. Such appearances are private revelations, which add nothing to the deposit of faith but may help us live it (CCC 67). Like Elijah and John, she is sent to prepare the way, and she points to her Son.
study: Who are the voices God has sent into my life whom I may not have recognised?
John suffered for telling the truth. Where does my faith ask for courage rather than comfort?

lead: This is Gaudete Sunday, named from the opening word of the Entrance Antiphon: Gaudete in Domino semper, “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4). The Lord is near, and the Church’s joy begins to break through the waiting. Rose vestments may be worn today.

Each reading gives one note of this joy. In Isaiah an anointed messenger brings good news to the oppressed, and Zion exults like a bride. In place of a psalm we sing the song of Mary, “my spirit rejoices in God my Savior”. St Paul writes, “Rejoice always”. And in John’s Gospel the Baptist tells us what kind of joy this is: he is not the light, he is not the Messiah, and he is glad to be only a voice for the one who stands among us unknown. The key words are anointed, rejoice and witness.

r.h: He has sent me to bring good news
set: Chapters 56–66 of Isaiah are usually dated after the return from Babylon, when the exiles had come home and found ruins and disappointment, not the glory they had hoped for. Into that discouragement a prophetic voice speaks, the voice of someone anointed by the Spirit.

The Lectionary makes two cuts. It stops in the middle of v. 2, at “the year of the Lord’s favor”, before “the day of vengeance”. Jesus stops at the same place when he reads this passage in Nazareth (Luke 4:18–19). It then goes to vv. 10–11, the joyful answer of Zion.
str: v. 1: the Spirit, the anointing and the mission.
v. 2a: the year of favour.
v. 10: the response: clothed in salvation, like a bridegroom and a bride.
v. 11: God will make justice spring up like plants in a garden.
kw: The word from which “Messiah” comes. Kings and priests were anointed with oil. This speaker is anointed with the Spirit.
The Greek Old Testament translates it with euangelizesthai, which gives us the word “Gospel”. The poor are the first to hear it.
The word used for the release proclaimed in the Jubilee year, every fiftieth year, when slaves went home and land was returned (Leviticus 25:10).
God’s saving justice, which sets things right. Here it is something that God clothes a person in, and something that grows like a plant.
vv: The spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the oppressed, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to the prisoners;
In Nazareth Jesus reads these words and says, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). “To bind up” is the word for bandaging a wound: this messenger is also a healer.
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor,
Jubilee language: a whole year of God’s mercy. In Christ it becomes a time of mercy that has no end.
I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my whole being shall exult in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness,
The joy comes from what has been received. Salvation is something we are dressed in, as at a wedding. Mary’s song, sung today, has the same movement: “my spirit rejoices in God”.
so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.
Growth is slow and hidden, like a seed in the ground. That is the way of God’s work in the small town of Nazareth, and in us.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ inaugurates the proclamation of the Good News by making this passage of Isaiah his own (CCC 714). The name “Christ” means “anointed” (CCC 436), and Christians share in that name through Baptism and Confirmation (CCC 1241, 1289). Each Christian is sent, then, to bring the same good news to the poor (see CCC 2443–2449 on love for the poor).

r.h: My spirit rejoices
set: Mary has travelled to visit Elizabeth, and Elizabeth has called her blessed (1:42–45). Mary answers with a song. Its language is drawn from the Old Testament, above all from the song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10), and from the Psalms. Mary sings as the voice of Israel, and also in her own voice as the handmaid who has been looked upon. The Lectionary uses part of it today as the response to the first reading, leaving out vv. 51–52 and 55.
str: vv. 46–48: personal praise: God has looked on his lowly servant.
vv. 49–50: the Mighty One, holy and merciful.
vv. 53–54: God turns things around and remembers Israel.
kw: To make great, to declare great. In Latin Magnificat, which gives the song its name.
A word for overflowing joy, often used in the Greek Psalms. It is the feeling of Isaiah 61:10.
Low estate, not simply a humble attitude. It is the word used of Hannah’s affliction (1 Samuel 1:11). God looks on those who are of no account.
vv: And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord,
and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
Mary calls God her Savior. The one preserved from sin knows better than anyone how much she owes him.
for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
This is a prophecy being fulfilled every time the Hail Mary is prayed. The praise is for what God has done, as the next verse says.
he has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty.
The verbs are in the past tense, as though it had already happened. God’s reversal has begun in the child Mary is carrying.
ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church (CCC 2619). The Latin Church sings it at every Evening Prayer. St Ambrose writes: let the soul of Mary be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and her spirit to rejoice in God (in substance). Because of vv. 52–53, this is also a song the Church cannot sing without care for the hungry.

r.h: Rejoice always
set: This is very likely the oldest writing in the New Testament, sent by Paul around AD 50–51, probably from Corinth. He had stayed only a short time in Thessalonica before being forced to leave (Acts 17:1–10), and he writes to a young Church that is suffering and asking about the Lord’s return. These verses come at the end of the letter, as a series of short commands.
str: vv. 16–18: three commands about the life of prayer: rejoice, pray, give thanks.
vv. 19–22: five commands about discernment of the Spirit’s gifts.
vv. 23–24: a prayer for holiness and the assurance that God is faithful.
kw: The word for something that goes on with no break. Paul uses it of his own prayer and thanks (1:3; 2:13). It does not mean endless words but a life that does not break its contact with God.
The word for putting out a fire or a lamp. The Spirit is like a fire, and Christians can dampen him by neglect or by contempt.
The word used for the arrival of a king or of an important visitor. This letter speaks of it several times (2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23).
vv: Rejoice always,
pray without ceasing,
give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
Paul says “in” all circumstances, not “for” all of them. He writes to people under persecution, and he is not asking them to pretend. Joy comes from what Christ has done.
Do not quench the Spirit.
but test everything; hold fast to what is good;
Enthusiasm needs discernment. The Catechism applies this to the discernment of charisms by the Church’s shepherds (CCC 801).
May the God of peace himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be kept sound and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do this.
The final word puts all the commands in their place. It is God who will do it.
ch: The Catechism takes “pray without ceasing” as the rule for Christian prayer (CCC 2742–2745), and quotes Origen: he prays without ceasing who unites prayer to works and good works to prayer. St Augustine teaches that it is desire that prays continually: if your desire is unbroken, so is your prayer (in substance). The Catechism also places “give thanks in all circumstances” at the heart of the prayer of thanksgiving (CCC 2638).

r.h: Among you stands one whom you do not know
set: The first passage comes from the great Prologue of John’s Gospel, which speaks of the Word and the light, and brings in John as “a man sent from God”. In this Gospel he is never called “the Baptist”: he is above all the witness. The second passage opens the story proper with an official enquiry.

When John the Evangelist writes “the Jews” here (v. 19), he means the religious authorities in Jerusalem, as v. 24 shows: “they had been sent from the Pharisees”. It does not mean the Jewish people. Jesus, John and all the first disciples were themselves Jews, and the Church teaches that blame must not be laid on the Jewish people (CCC 597–598). An enquiry was a reasonable thing to make. They had a duty to look into someone stirring up crowds in the wilderness and using a rite of washing.
str: vv. 6–8: John, the witness to the light.
vv. 19–21: Who are you? He says three times what he is not: not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the prophet.
vv. 22–23: What do you say about yourself? “The voice”.
vv. 24–25: Why then do you baptize?
vv. 26–28: one is standing among you, greater than I; the place: Bethany across the Jordan.
kw: A word from the law court, and a central one for this Gospel. A witness says what he has seen and points away from himself. Later this word gives us “martyr”.
John takes the words of Isaiah 40:3 as his identity. A voice has no message of its own; it carries the word.
In John’s Gospel this often means the leaders at Jerusalem, as it does here. It can also mean the people of Judea, and sometimes it is said with favour (4:22).
vv: He himself was not the light, but he came to testify to the light.
A sentence that could be the motto of every priest, catechist and parent.
He confessed and did not deny it, but confessed, “I am not the Messiah.”
A solemn statement. Many commentators set this “I am not” (egō ouk eimi) against Jesus’ “I am” sayings later in the Gospel.
And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the prophet?” He answered, “No.”
Each answer is shorter than the one before. “The prophet” means the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18.
He said, “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’” as the prophet Isaiah said.
John answered them, “I baptize with water. Among you stands one whom you do not know,
This is the Gospel’s Advent message. The one we wait for is already among us, not yet recognised.
the one who is coming after me; I am not worthy to untie the thong of his sandal.”
Untying sandals was the task of a slave. A later Jewish saying holds that a disciple should do everything for his teacher except this. John considers himself unworthy even of that.
This took place in Bethany across the Jordan where John was baptizing.

A note on the text. This is not the Bethany of Lazarus, near Jerusalem. Origen could not find this place and preferred the reading “Bethabara”, which is found in some manuscripts. The oldest manuscripts have Bethany.
ch: The Catechism says that John, by his preaching and by his baptism, prepares the way, and is the Lord’s immediate forerunner (CCC 523). St Augustine draws out the contrast: John is the voice for a time, and Christ is the eternal Word; the voice passes, once it has brought the Word to the heart, and the Word remains (in substance). This is why John says later, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). That is the joy of Gaudete Sunday: to be glad that it is not about us.

qa: Jesus says John is Elijah (Matthew 11:14), and John says he is not. Which is right?
Both. John denies being the historical Elijah returned in person. Jesus means that he comes “with the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). So St Gregory the Great explains it (in substance).
Does Paul teach that man has three parts: spirit, soul and body?

The Catechism says that this distinction does not introduce a duality into the soul. “Spirit” signifies that from creation we are ordered to a supernatural end (CCC 367). Paul’s point here is that God wants to sanctify the whole person.
How can Paul command joy? Feelings cannot be ordered.

Christian joy is not a mood. It is what comes from the fact that the Lord has come and will come again, and it can stay alongside tears. Paul writes this to people under persecution, and he himself knew prison and beatings. That is why it is set beside prayer and thanksgiving, which can be chosen.
rite: In the Roman Rite this Sunday marks a change within Advent. Rose vestments may replace violet, and the third candle of the Advent wreath, often rose in colour, is lit. Advent has two parts: until 16 December the prayers look more to the Lord’s final coming, and from 17 December they prepare more directly for Christmas. Today’s readings stand close to that turning point. Because 13 December this year falls on a Sunday, the memorial of St Lucy is not kept as it would be on a weekday, but her name, which is connected with “light”, fits with a Gospel about one who testifies to the light.
study: John says first what he is not. What false claims do I need to give up in order to point to Christ?
Paul’s three commands in 5:16–18 are for all circumstances. Which is the hardest for me this week?
“Among you stands one whom you do not know.” Where might Christ be standing unrecognised in my family or parish?
Isaiah’s messenger is sent to the oppressed and the brokenhearted. Who are they in my own place, and what good news can I bring them before Christmas?

lead: A foreign seer, hired to curse Israel, finds that he can only bless, and he sees far ahead: “a star shall come out of Jacob”. In the Gospel the leaders of the Temple ask Jesus by what authority he acts, and he answers them with a question about John. The psalm prays, “Make me to know your ways, O Lord.” One man from outside Israel sees truly by God’s gift, while some leaders of the Temple decline to say what they see.

r.h: A star shall come out of Jacob
set: Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, near the end of the desert journey. Balak, king of Moab, is afraid and hires Balaam, a well-known seer from the east, to curse them (Numbers 22–24). Three times he tries, and each time blessing comes out of his mouth. Our reading gives parts of his third and fourth oracles. Scripture elsewhere judges him severely for what he did afterward (Numbers 31:16; Revelation 2:14), but here God uses him as a true prophet.
str: vv. 2–4: the spirit of God comes on him; he describes himself as a seer.
vv. 5–7: a blessing on Israel’s tents, with pictures of water and gardens.
vv. 15–16: the opening of the last oracle.
v. 17a: the vision: a star and a scepter.
kw: A solemn word for a divine utterance, usually said of the Lord’s own prophets. Here it is in the mouth of a foreigner.
In the ancient Near East a star was a sign of a king or of a god. In Israel’s later hope this verse came to be read as speaking of the Messiah.
The ruler’s staff, parallel with “star”. It may look first to David, who defeated Moab (2 Samuel 8:2), and then beyond him. See also Genesis 49:10.
vv: how fair are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!
Balaam looks at a camp of desert tents and sees a garden. He is seeing what God sees.
I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near
The most mysterious line of the oracle. The seer truly sees, but from far away. Advent lives in that “not now”, and Christmas is the answer to it.
a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel;
The Greek Old Testament has “a man shall rise” in place of “a scepter”, which shows how early this verse was read as speaking of a person.
ch: St Justin and St Irenaeus read this star as Christ himself (in substance). The Church connects it with the star of the Magi (Matthew 2:2), who like Balaam came from the east. Origen thought that the Magi knew of Balaam’s prophecy (in substance). The Catechism sees the Magi as the first of the nations to come to Christ (CCC 528). The Book of Revelation calls Jesus “the bright morning star” (22:16).

r.h: By what authority?
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem in triumph and has driven out the sellers from the Temple (21:1–17). Now he is teaching in the Temple courts, and the people responsible for it come to question him. They are a small group of leaders, the chief priests and the elders. Their question is a natural one: who permitted these actions?
str: v. 23: the question: By what authority?
vv. 24–25a: Jesus’ counter-question about John’s baptism.
vv. 25b–26: the leaders’ private reasoning.
v. 27: “We do not know”; “Neither will I tell you”.
kw: Right and power to act. Matthew has already said that Jesus taught “as one having authority” (7:29), and at the end the risen Lord will say “All authority” has been given him (28:18).
A reverent way of saying “from God”, which was common among Jews of that time.
vv: “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?”
Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin?”
Answering a question with a question was a familiar way of teaching. It is also a true reply: the one who could accept John’s call would know where Jesus’ authority comes from.
So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.”
They do not say this because they have looked and could not tell, but because of the consequences. Those who will not say what they think cannot receive any further answer.
ch: The Catechism explains that Jesus taught with an authority that went beyond the interpretation of the Law of his time, not as the scribes (CCC 581), and carefully says that the charges made by some leaders must never be laid on Jews in general (CCC 597). The question is one for each of us: do we ask about Jesus’ authority to obey it, or only to keep it at a distance?

qa: How could God speak through a pagan seer like Balaam?
God can use anyone. Nothing about the gift of prophecy makes the prophet holy, and Scripture does not hide Balaam’s failings. God’s word stays true even when his messenger is flawed.
rite: Today is the memorial of St John of the Cross (1542–1591), a Spanish Carmelite priest, who worked with St Teresa of Avila on the reform of their Order. Members of his own Order imprisoned him in Toledo in 1577–78, and in that dark cell he composed much of his great poem, the Spiritual Canticle. He wrote of the “dark night”, in which God draws the soul closer by means that it cannot yet see. He died at Úbeda on 14 December 1591, and Pius XI declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1926. Balaam’s star, seen “not now” and “not near”, suits him well. The Catechism quotes his saying: “At the evening of life, we shall be judged on our love” (CCC 1022).
study: Balaam saw truly, “but not now”. What promise of God am I still waiting for, seeing it only from far away?
When have I, like the leaders in today’s Gospel, said “I do not know” in order to avoid a truth I did not want to face?

lead: In the last days before Christmas the Church looks for the people who will be ready to receive the Lord. Zephaniah sees a proud city purified until only a humble and lowly people remains. In the Gospel Jesus tells the chief priests and elders of two sons: the one who said no and then went, and the one who said yes and stayed at home. Both readings ask the same Advent question: who is really ready? Psalm 34 gives the answer in one line: “The Lord hears the cry of the poor.”

r.h: A people humble and lowly
set: Zephaniah preached in Judah in the days of King Josiah (1:1), who reigned from about 640 to 609 BC. His book opens with the day of the Lord, “a day of wrath” (1:15), the line from which the medieval hymn Dies Irae takes its first words. Chapter 3 begins with a cry against an unnamed “oppressing city”; the context shows that it is Jerusalem herself. The lectionary passes over vv. 3–8, the charge against her officials, judges, prophets and priests, and moves straight from the sin to the promise.
str: vv. 1–2: the city that listens to no one and does not draw near to God.
vv. 9–10: the nations, with purified speech, call on the Lord and bring him offerings.
vv. 11–13: the proud are removed; a humble remnant is left, and it lives in peace.
kw: Literally “a purified lip”. The noun is the one used for the single language at Babel (Genesis 11:1). What pride divided there, God now heals, so that all may call on one Name.

‘Ānî means poor, afflicted, bent low; dal means weak, of no account. Earlier the prophet called “all you humble of the land” to seek the Lord (2:3). This is the root of what later piety calls the poor of the Lord.
What remains when the rest is gone. God's plan does not depend on large numbers but on a faithful few who carry the promise.
vv: At that time I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, that all of them may call on the name of the Lord and serve him with one accord.
The promise reaches beyond Israel. The judgment on Jerusalem does not end in ruin but in worship by all peoples together.
For I will leave in the midst of you a people humble and lowly.
God removes the “proudly exultant” (v. 11), and those who remain have nothing to boast of. Their only security is the next line: they seek refuge in the name of the Lord.
they shall do no wrong and utter no lies, nor shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouths.
Humility is not weakness of character. It produces truthfulness. Revelation uses the same picture for the redeemed who follow the Lamb: “in their mouth no lie was found” (Revelation 14:5).
ch: The Catechism sees in this remnant the bearers of Israel's hope: “the poor and humble of the Lord” (CCC 64), who converge with the promises of the Messiah and of the Spirit (CCC 711) and are “the great achievement” of the Spirit's hidden mission (CCC 716). The Second Vatican Council places Mary at the head of them: she “stands out among the poor and humble of the Lord” (Lumen Gentium 55). That is why this reading belongs to Advent: it describes the people among whom Christ would be born.

r.h: The son who changed his mind
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem and cleansed the temple. As he teaches there, “the chief priests and the elders of the people” ask by what authority he acts, and he answers with a question about John the Baptist, which they refuse to answer (21:23–27). This parable follows at once. It is the first of three addressed to these leaders; the wicked tenants and the wedding banquet come next. The vineyard is an old image for God's people (Isaiah 5:1–7).
str: vv. 28–30: two sons, two answers, two actions.
v. 31a: the question: which one did the father's will?
vv. 31b–32: the application: the tax collectors and prostitutes believed John, and his hearers in authority did not.
kw: to change one's mind, to regret
The word appears in v. 29 of the first son and again in v. 32, where Jesus says the leaders “did not change” their minds. The whole parable turns on this one verb.
“Righteousness” in Matthew is a life that does God's will (compare 5:6; 6:33). John both preached this way and walked in it.
A present tense. Jesus does not say the door is shut on his hearers. Others have gone in first, and the way is still open.
vv: He answered, ‘I will not’; but later he changed his mind and went.

A note on the text. Ancient manuscripts differ in the order of the two sons. Many have the order of the NRSV: the first refuses and then goes. Others, including Codex Vaticanus, reverse it: the first says yes and does not go, the second refuses and then goes, and the answer in v. 31 changes to match. The Malayalam POC follows that second order. The meaning is the same in both.
Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God ahead of you.

Tax collectors worked for the occupying power and were despised as traitors and cheats; prostitutes were shunned. Jesus does not praise their sins. He praises what they did when they heard John: they believed and turned.
and even after you saw it, you did not change your minds and believe him.
The leaders had a second chance. They could have watched sinners being changed and been moved by it. To see God at work in others and still not turn is the saddest part of the story.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom (CCC 545) and that the prayer of faith is not only saying “Lord, Lord” but disposing the heart to do the Father's will (CCC 2611). Interior conversion, a radical turning back to God, is the heart of the Christian life (CCC 1430–1431). St Paul suggests a last word on the two sons: there is a third Son whose word and deed are one, for in him every one of God's promises is a “Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

qa: Is Jesus rejecting the Jewish people here?

No. He is speaking to “the chief priests and the elders of the people” (21:23) in a particular dispute over John. The tax collectors and prostitutes who believed were Jews too, and so were John and Jesus himself. The Church firmly rejects any blame laid on the Jewish people as such (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
study: Where in my life have I said “I go, sir” and not gone? Where have I said no, and is it still possible to change my mind and go?
Zephaniah's remnant has only one security, the name of the Lord. What do I rely on instead as Christmas comes near?

lead: Today's first reading gives Advent one of its best-known prayers: “Shower, O heavens, from above.” The God who alone is God promises that righteousness will come down and salvation spring up, and he calls all the ends of the earth to turn to him. In the Gospel John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the one to come, and Jesus answers by pointing to what is happening: the blind see, and the poor hear good news. Prophecy asks; the Gospel answers.

r.h: Let the skies rain down righteousness
set: Isaiah 40–55 speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon. Chapter 45 opens with an astonishing oracle: God calls Cyrus, the Persian king who took Babylon in 539 BC, “his anointed” (45:1), even though Cyrus does not know him (45:4–5). Today's verses draw the conclusion. If the Lord can use a foreign king to bring his people home, he is not one god among many. He is the Creator, and there is no other.
str: vv. 6b–7: “I am the Lord, and there is no other”: light and darkness, weal and woe are all under him.
v. 8: the prayer and promise: heaven rains down, earth opens.
v. 18: God made the earth to be lived in, not as a chaos.
vv. 21b–25: the only Saviour invites all the ends of the earth; every knee shall bow.
kw: God's saving faithfulness, his setting things right, more than a legal verdict. In v. 8 it falls like rain and also sprouts from the ground: it is God's gift, and the earth receives it and bears it.

The word of Genesis 1:2, “a formless void”. In v. 18 God says he did not create the earth for that. To exiles whose world had collapsed, this is a word of hope: God's purpose is a home for his people.
From the same Hebrew root as the name Yeshua, Jesus. In v. 21 God claims this title for himself alone.
vv: I form light and create darkness, I make weal and create woe; I the Lord do all these things.
This is a statement of God's sovereignty over all that happens, not a claim that he does moral evil. The Hebrew words are šālôm (peace, well-being) and ra‘ (here misfortune, disaster).
Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the skies rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation may spring up

The Latin Vulgate reads the abstract nouns as a person: the clouds rain down “the Just One” and the earth brings forth “a Saviour”. From that wording comes the Advent chant Rorate caeli and today's psalm refrain. Heaven and earth meet: the gift comes from above, and it grows from below.
Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other.
Because there is only one God, salvation cannot belong to one nation only. Israel's faith in one God opens outward to the whole world.
“To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.”

St Paul applies these words to Jesus: “at the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Philippians 2:10; see also Romans 14:11). It is one of the strongest signs of the earliest Christian faith in Christ's divinity: words spoken by the Lord God are said of him.
ch: The Church has made Isaiah 45:8 her Advent prayer: it is the Entrance Antiphon of the Fourth Sunday of Advent and the source of the chant Rorate caeli. The Catechism teaches on v. 7's question that God is in no way, directly or indirectly, the cause of moral evil, though he permits it and can draw good from it (CCC 311).

r.h: Are you the one who is to come?
set: At the end of chapter 3 Luke told us that Herod had shut John up in prison (3:20), and Matthew says plainly that John asks this question from prison (Matthew 11:2). John had announced one who would come with winnowing fork and fire (Luke 3:16–17). His disciples now report what Jesus is doing: he has healed the centurion's servant and raised the widow's son at Nain (7:1–17). This is mercy, not the fire John spoke of. So John asks.
str: vv. 18b–20: John sends two disciples with his question, and they repeat it word for word.
v. 21: Luke's note: Jesus was healing many at that very moment.
v. 22: the answer: go and tell John what you have seen and heard.
v. 23: a beatitude for those who do not stumble.
kw: the one who is to come
A title of expectation, drawn from such texts as Psalm 118:26 and Malachi 3:1. John himself used the verb of the one more powerful than he (3:16).
The last item on the list and its climax, in the words of Isaiah 61:1, which Jesus read out at Nazareth (Luke 4:18).
A skandalon is a stumbling block. People may stumble over a Messiah who does not match their expectations.
vv: Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?
This is the question of Advent itself, and Luke does not hide that it comes from the greatest of the prophets.
Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news brought to them.

Jesus gives no title and makes no claim. He weaves together Isaiah's pictures of the age to come (Isaiah 29:18–19; 35:5–6; 61:1), and John, who knows the Scriptures, will understand. Lepers and the dead are added to what those passages list.
And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.
A gentle word for John and for us. God's way may not be the way we expected. Blessed are those who go on trusting.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' signs attest that the Father has sent him and invite belief, but that they can also be an occasion for offense (CCC 547–549). It calls John the Lord's immediate forerunner (CCC 523). St John Chrysostom held that John asked for his disciples' sake, to send them to Jesus, and not from doubt of his own (in substance). Many modern readers hear also the real question of a man in prison. Either way, the answer is the same, and it is meant for everyone who has ever asked.

qa: Does Isaiah 45:7 mean God creates evil?

No. “Woe” here means disaster and hardship, in a sentence asserting that nothing lies outside God's rule, against any idea of a rival god of darkness. The Church teaches that God is in no way the cause of moral evil (CCC 311).
study: John had to let Jesus be different from what he expected. Where has God not matched my expectations, and how have I responded?
If someone asked me whether Jesus is really the one, what could I honestly point to, as Jesus pointed to the blind and the poor?

lead: From today until Christmas Eve the Mass readings change their tone: Advent now prepares directly for the birth of Christ. The Church begins at the roots. On his deathbed Jacob promises that the scepter shall not depart from Judah, and Matthew opens his Gospel with the family tree in which that promise runs on, through saints and sinners, to Jesus the Messiah, “the son of David, the son of Abraham.” Psalm 72 sings of the king in whose time justice shall flourish.

r.h: The scepter shall not depart from Judah
set: Genesis is ending. Jacob, also called Israel, is dying in Egypt and gathers his twelve sons to tell them what will happen “in days to come” (49:1). The poem is called his blessing, though the first three sons, Reuben, Simeon and Levi, hear hard words (49:3–7). Judah, the fourth, is next, and he receives the leadership. Later history is read in this poem: David and his royal line came from the tribe of Judah.
str: v. 2: Jacob calls his sons to listen.
v. 8: Judah praised by his brothers, victorious over his enemies.
v. 9: the lion.
v. 10: the scepter and the promise of one to come.
kw: A staff or rod, the sign of a ruler. It can also mean a tribe. In v. 10 it is paired with the “ruler's staff” held between the feet of an enthroned king.
A young lion, strong and fearless. The New Testament takes up the image: “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).
The most disputed phrase of the poem; see the note under v. 10.
vv: Judah, your brothers shall praise you
A play on words. Judah (Yehudah) sounds like the verb “to praise” (yādâ), as Leah said at his birth: “This time I will praise the Lord” (29:35).
The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and the obedience of the peoples is his.

A note on the text. The Hebrew phrase is obscure and has been read in several ways. It could be “until Shiloh comes”, which the Hebrew letters most directly suggest; “until tribute comes to him”, as the NRSV has it, by a small change in reading; or “until he comes to whom it belongs”, close to the Malayalam POC's “its heir”. The Latin Vulgate has “until he comes who is to be sent”. Many ancient readers felt that the verse looks forward to a ruler still to come.
ch: Ancient Jewish interpreters read this verse of the king to come; the Aramaic Targum Onkelos names the Messiah here. Christians read it of Jesus, who “was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14). St Justin Martyr used it in his First Apology to show that the Messiah had been foretold (in substance). The last words of the verse are wider than Israel: “the obedience of the peoples”. The Church hears that fulfilled when Jesus is confessed among the nations.

r.h: The book of the origin of Jesus Christ
set: Matthew wrote for a Church deeply rooted in Israel's Scriptures, and his first page is a list of names. To a modern reader it seems dull; to his first readers it was a claim. Family trees established who a person was and what he could inherit. This one says that Jesus is the heir of the promises made to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16).
str: v. 1: the title.
vv. 2–6a: Abraham to David, rising to the kingship.
vv. 6b–11: David to the deportation to Babylon, falling to disaster.
vv. 12–16: the deportation to Jesus, in obscurity, with most of the names otherwise unknown.
v. 17: the summary: three sets of fourteen.
kw: The phrase of the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. It could also be heard as “the book of the origin”. Matthew's first words recall the first book of the Bible: something new is beginning.
The Greek for the Hebrew Mashiach, the anointed one. Here it is not yet simply a surname: it is the claim that Jesus is the anointed king Israel was waiting for.

Matthew reaches this number with some selection: three kings between Joram and Uzziah are omitted (compare 1 Chronicles 3:11–12). Many scholars suggest a reason: in Hebrew the letters of David's name, DWD, add up to fourteen. If that is correct, the whole list is signed with David's name.
vv: An account of the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
Two names, two promises. David stands for the kingdom, Abraham for the blessing of all nations. Matthew ends where he begins: “make disciples of all nations” (28:19).
and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar

Genealogies usually name only fathers. Matthew names four women before Mary: Tamar (v. 3), Rahab and Ruth (v. 5), and “the wife of Uriah” (v. 6). Rahab was of Jericho, Ruth of Moab, and Uriah a Hittite; each of their stories is irregular or painful. God's plan passes through foreigners and through wounded histories.
and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.
The pattern “A the father of B” breaks here. In Greek “of whom” is feminine, and refers to Mary alone. Joseph is the legal link to David, and Mary is the mother. Tomorrow's Gospel explains why.
ch: St Leo the Great, in a letter used in the Office of Readings today, says that to call the Lord true man would be of no value to us unless we believe he comes from the line of ancestors the Gospel sets out (in substance). The list guards the truth of the Incarnation: God entered a real family. The Catechism notes that Joseph was called so that Jesus should be born “into the messianic lineage of David” (CCC 437). The women point ahead too: the mission of many holy women prepared for Mary's, and God chooses those considered weak to show his faithfulness (CCC 489).

qa: Why do Matthew and Luke give different genealogies of Jesus?

Luke 3:23–38 has a different list between David and Joseph. Neither Gospel explains this. An early explanation, by Julius Africanus and preserved by Eusebius, appeals to levirate marriage; others suggest that one list is legal and the other natural. No solution is certain. Both Gospels agree on what matters: Jesus belongs to David's line, and his conception is the work of God.
rite: From 17 December the Roman Rite sings the “O Antiphons”, one each evening at the Magnificat of Vespers and also used before the Gospel at Mass. Today's is O Sapientia, “O Wisdom”. Each one calls on Christ by an Old Testament title and ends with “Come”.
study: Whose names would appear in my own story of faith, including the painful ones? Can I see God at work through them?
Matthew does not hide the sinners among Jesus' ancestors. How does that change the way I think about my own family and my parish?

lead: Yesterday's genealogy ended with a puzzle: Joseph, of David's line, is the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. Today's Gospel explains it. An angel tells Joseph to take Mary home and to give the child his name, and so Jesus becomes a son of David through Joseph. Jeremiah supplies the promise behind the story: a righteous Branch for David, called “The Lord is our righteousness.” Joseph, the righteous man, stands at the point where that promise is kept.

r.h: A righteous Branch for David
set: Jeremiah preached in Jerusalem in the last decades before its fall in 587 BC. In 21:11 to 23:4 he gives his judgment on the kings of Judah, whom he calls shepherds who scattered the flock (23:1–2). The last of them was Zedekiah, whose name means “The Lord is my righteousness”. Today's oracle comes straight after that judgment: God himself will give a true king.
str: v. 5: the promise of the Branch: he reigns, acts wisely, does justice.
v. 6: the results (Judah saved, Israel safe) and his name.
vv. 7–8: a new exodus, greater than the first.
kw: Ṣemaḥ is a shoot growing up from what seems dead. Zechariah uses the same word as a title for the one to come (Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). The Greek Old Testament renders it anatolē, which also means “rising, dawn”, a word that returns in Luke 1:78.
The twin duties of a king in the Bible: to give right judgment and to protect the weak. Jeremiah charged the kings of his time with failing in this (22:13–17).
The name turns Zedekiah's name around, using the same words. Zedekiah did not live up to his name. The true king will, and “my” becomes “our”.
vv: The days are surely coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch
The dynasty looked like a felled tree. God promises new growth, from the same root and by his own act: “I will raise up”.
In his days Judah will be saved and Israel will live in safety.
Both halves of the divided people are named. The northern kingdom had been gone for over a century; the promised king will restore all of them.
Then they shall live in their own land.

Israel's oath will change. They used to swear by the God who brought them out of Egypt, and they will swear by the God who brought them home from every land. A return would be counted as great as the Exodus.
ch: Christians read the Branch as Jesus, the son of David, in whom God's justice comes to the earth. St Paul says that Christ “became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30): the name in Jeremiah finds its meaning in him. The Catechism teaches that the kingdom promised to David would be the work of the Spirit and would belong to the poor according to the Spirit (CCC 709).

r.h: Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid
set: A Jewish betrothal in that time was more than an engagement: the couple were legally husband and wife, and only divorce could end it, though they did not yet live together. That is why Matthew calls Joseph “her husband” and speaks of dismissing her. Unlike Luke, Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side.
str: v. 18: the fact: Mary is with child from the Holy Spirit.
v. 19: Joseph's decision.
vv. 20–21: the dream: take her, and name him.
vv. 22–23: Matthew's first fulfillment text.
vv. 24–25: Joseph does exactly what he was told.
kw: Joseph keeps God's law, and his law-keeping has mercy in it: he will not expose her to shame. The same quality marks the “righteous Branch” in today's first reading.
The Greek for Yeshua, “the Lord saves” (CCC 430). In that culture the father gave the name, and by doing so accepted the child as his own. By naming him, Joseph makes him legally a son of David.
From Isaiah 7:14. Matthew frames his whole Gospel with this promise, for Jesus' last words are “I am with you always” (28:20).
vv: Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.

The Fathers discussed what was in Joseph's mind. St Jerome thought that Joseph, knowing Mary's chastity and amazed at what had happened, kept silent about a mystery he did not understand (in substance). Others read it as mercy toward her in a painful doubt. Both readings honour him.
She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.
Not from Rome, as many might have hoped, but from sin. The mission is in the name. The Catechism takes this verse as the summary of the Gospel: God's mercy to sinners (CCC 1846).
“Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall name him Emmanuel,”

The Hebrew of Isaiah 7:14 has ‘almâ, “young woman”, and the Greek Old Testament, which Matthew quotes, has parthenos, “virgin”. Matthew reads the text in the light of what has happened, and the Church sees in the virginal conception the fulfillment of the promise (CCC 497).
ch: The Catechism says that Joseph was called so that Jesus should be born of his spouse “into the messianic lineage of David” (CCC 437). It teaches that the virginal conception is a divine work surpassing human understanding (CCC 497), and that the Church confesses Mary's perpetual virginity (CCC 499–501). St John Paul II, in Redemptoris Custos (1989), presents Joseph as the guardian of the Redeemer, a man whose obedience of faith is seen in what he does; the Gospels record no word of his.

qa: Does “until she had borne a son” (1:25) mean Joseph and Mary later had marital relations?

No. In biblical language “until” says what happened up to a certain point and implies nothing about what came after. St Paul says that Christ “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25), and his reign will not stop then. St Jerome made this point against Helvidius. The verse protects the virginal conception, and the Church confesses Mary as ever-virgin (CCC 499–501).
rite: Today's O Antiphon is O Adonai, the title by which Jewish reading replaces the holy Name. It recalls the Lord who appeared to Moses in the burning bush and gave him the Law on Sinai. The name Jesus, given today, carries that same Name within it: “the Lord saves”.
study: Joseph obeyed without saying a word. Which instruction from God do I keep discussing instead of doing?
Jesus came to save us from our sins. Do I really want that salvation this Christmas, or some other?

lead: Two barren women, two angels, two sons set apart before their birth. The reading from Judges and the Gospel of Luke are told almost in the same words, and the Church places them side by side on purpose. God begins his great deliverances where human hope has run out. Samson will “begin to deliver” Israel; John will prepare a people for the Lord himself. Psalm 71 is the prayer of one who has relied on God “from my mother's womb”.

r.h: The birth of Samson is announced
set: The Book of Judges tells a repeated story: Israel does evil, falls under an enemy, cries out, and God raises up a deliverer. Chapter 13 opens with Israel forty years under the Philistines (13:1), and this time no cry is recorded. God acts first. The scene is a small home of the tribe of Dan, in Zorah, in the foothills west of Jerusalem.
str: v. 2: Manoah and his barren wife, who is never named.
vv. 3–5: the angel's message: a son, a nazirite, a beginning of deliverance.
vv. 6–7: she tells her husband.
vv. 24–25a: the birth, the name, the first stirring of the Spirit.
kw: The same word is used of Sarah, Rebekah and Rachel (Genesis 11:30; 25:21; 29:31). In Israel's story it signals that a child will be God's gift and a turning point in the history of his people.

Numbers 6:1–21 describes a vow by which a man or woman is consecrated to God for a time: no wine, no razor, no touching a dead body. Samson's case is unusual, since the consecration is lifelong and starts before birth, and it binds his mother as well.
God's messenger, in whom God himself is often felt to be present. The woman describes him as “most awe-inspiring” (13:6).
vv: “Although you are barren, having borne no children, you shall conceive and bear a son.
The form of the announcement is a fixed one in Scripture: appearance, promise, name or mission. The same form returns today in Luke, and tomorrow for Mary.
It is he who shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.

Only “begin”. Samson's life, read on in chapters 14 to 16, is a strange mixture of strength and failure, and the Philistines are still there at the end. Israel's real deliverance lies ahead. The Letter to the Hebrews still numbers him among those of faith (Hebrews 11:32).
The woman bore a son, and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the Lord blessed him.
A quiet sentence very like the ones Luke uses of John and of Jesus (Luke 1:80; 2:40).
ch: The Catechism sees in such women the preparation for Mary: against all human expectation God chooses those who were considered powerless and weak to show his faithfulness (CCC 489). Samson is thus a figure in the old sense: he points beyond himself. His consecration from the womb and his partial deliverance prepare us to hear of one who will be greater.

r.h: The birth of John the Baptist is announced
set: After a short preface (1:1–4), Luke begins his Gospel in the temple in Jerusalem, and he will end it there (24:53). “Herod” is Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC. David's arrangement divided the priests into twenty-four orders, each serving in turn; Abijah's was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10). There were many priests, so the task of offering incense was given by lot, and later Jewish tradition suggests that a priest might have it only once in his life. So this is the greatest hour of Zechariah's life, and God meets him in it.
str: vv. 5–7: the couple: righteous, childless, old.
vv. 8–10: the hour of incense, with the people praying outside.
vv. 11–17: the angel: your prayer has been heard; a son named John.
vv. 18–20: Zechariah's question and the sign.
vv. 21–25: the people wait, he comes out mute; Elizabeth conceives.
kw: The Hebrew meanings are widely noted: Zechariah, “the Lord has remembered”; Elizabeth, “my God has sworn” or “my God is an oath”; John, “the Lord is gracious”. Put together, they almost tell the story.

Probably “God is my strength” or “mighty one of God”. In Daniel he comes at the time of the evening offering to explain the time of salvation (Daniel 8:16; 9:21). That he appears now tells the reader that the time has come.
the spirit and power of Elijah
Malachi ends the prophets with the promise that Elijah will return and “turn the hearts of parents to their children” (Malachi 4:5–6). The angel quotes that promise.
vv: Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John.
They may have stopped praying for a child long ago. God has not forgotten. An old prayer can be answered at a time when no one is expecting it.
With the spirit and power of Elijah he will go before him
“Him” here is the Lord God of v. 16. John goes before God. By the end of the story, the one who comes after John is Jesus. Luke is saying something tremendous about who Jesus is, with no fuss at all.
“How will I know that this is so? For I am an old man, and my wife is getting on in years.”
Abraham asked something similar (Genesis 15:8). But the angel takes it as unbelief (v. 20), and the priest who should have blessed the waiting people (Numbers 6:22–27) comes out unable to speak.
“This is what the Lord has done for me when he looked favorably on me and took away the disgrace I have endured among my people.”
Elizabeth, who is given no angel, is the first in this Gospel to praise God for what he has done. Childlessness in her world was felt as a public shame, and she names it, and names its end.
ch: The Catechism says that John was filled with the Holy Spirit “even from his mother's womb” (CCC 717), that he is Elijah who must come (CCC 718) and that he is the Lord's immediate forerunner (CCC 523). The Church keeps his birthday as a solemnity on 24 June, a rare honour: besides the Lord, only Mary and John have their earthly birth kept in the Roman calendar.

qa: Why was Zechariah punished for his question and Mary not for hers?

The words are close, but Luke marks a difference. Zechariah asks for proof, “How will I know?”, and the angel names it unbelief (1:20). Mary asks how it will come about, “How can this be?”, and then gives her consent (1:34, 38). Fathers such as St Ambrose see this difference (in substance). And Zechariah's silence ends in praise: when his tongue is released, his first words are a blessing (1:64).
rite: Today's O Antiphon is O Radix Jesse, “O Root of Jesse”, from Isaiah 11:1, 10. It fits a day of barren women: a root seems dead, and God brings life from it.
study: Is there an old prayer I have stopped praying because it seems too late? What would it mean to bring it back to God this Advent?
Elizabeth gives thanks in hiddenness for five months. Where could I use some quiet in these last days before Christmas, to see what the Lord has done for me?

lead: On the last Sunday of Advent the readings speak of a house. David, settled in his palace of cedar, wants to build a house for God, and God answers through Nathan with a promise: “the Lord will make you a house”, a royal line whose throne will last forever. In the Gospel that promise reaches a young woman in Nazareth: her son will receive “the throne of his ancestor David”, and God will come to dwell not in cedar but in her womb.

St Paul's short hymn of praise stands between them and names what is happening: a mystery kept secret for long ages is now disclosed. Psalm 89 sings the Lord's covenant with David. The key words of the day are house, promise and consent: God builds, God promises, and a human being says yes.

r.h: The Lord will make you a house
set: David has become king of all Israel, has taken Jerusalem, and has brought the ark of God there with dancing (2 Samuel 5–6). The wandering years are over. It seems only right that God's ark should have a home at least as fine as the king's. This chapter, known as the oracle of Nathan, is one of the foundation texts of Israel's hope for a Messiah. The Psalms sing it (Psalm 89; 132), and the Chronicler retells it (1 Chronicles 17).
str: vv. 1–3: David's plan, and Nathan's first approval.
vv. 4–5: that night God speaks: “Are you the one to build me a house to live in?”
vv. 8b–11a: what God has done and will do: from the pasture to the throne, a place for the people.
vv. 11b–12: the great reversal: the Lord will make David a house, and raise up his offspring.
vv. 14a, 16: father and son; a throne forever.

¶ The lectionary omits vv. 6–7, on God's having moved about in a tent, and v. 13, on the offspring who will build a house for God's name. David's son Solomon built the temple, but the promise goes well beyond him (see 1 Kings 8:19–20).
kw: The whole passage is built on this word's three meanings: a palace (v. 2), a temple (v. 5), a dynasty (v. 11). David wants to build God a temple; God promises David a family line. The Malayalam POC renders each by its sense, so the play on one word is lost there, and it is worth explaining.
The Lord has given David “rest” (vv. 1, 11). Rest in the land was the goal of the Exodus (Deuteronomy 12:9–10). God has been faithful, and now he goes further.
Used of the throne in v. 16. No human dynasty lasts forever. The word pushed Israel, after the kings had gone, to look ahead for a greater son of David.
vv: “See now, I am living in a house of cedar, but the ark of God stays in a tent.”
A generous thought, and Nathan at first agrees. But David is thinking as kings do: a god whose temple I built is in some sense my god. The Lord will not be housed by anyone.
Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
In the Hebrew the “you” stands out. Solomon's own prayer will say the same thing at the dedication: “Even heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you” (1 Kings 8:27).
I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep to be prince over my people Israel
God reminds David of where he began. Everything is a gift. The promised son of David will also be a shepherd.
Moreover the Lord declares to you that the Lord will make you a house.
The heart of the reading. Biblical faith runs in this direction: before we do anything for God, God does something for us. On Advent's last Sunday this is the whole message of Christmas.
I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me.
The king was called God's son in an adoptive sense (CCC 441). The Letter to the Hebrews applies this very line to Christ, in a far fuller sense (Hebrews 1:5).
Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me; your throne shall be established forever.
“Made sure” (Hebrew ne’man) comes from the root of “amen”, to be firm, reliable. The promise is as sure as God himself.
ch: St Augustine devotes part of Book XVII of the City of God to this promise and argues that it was not fulfilled in Solomon but in Christ (in substance). The Catechism notes that the temple David wished to build was the work of his son (CCC 2580), and that the kingdom promised to David would be the work of the Holy Spirit and would belong to the poor according to the Spirit (CCC 709). Gabriel's words in today's Gospel take up the promise phrase by phrase: great name, throne, house, son, forever.

r.h: The mystery now disclosed
set: This is the closing doxology of Paul's greatest letter, a single long sentence of praise. It sums up the letter's themes: the gospel, the Scriptures, all the Gentiles, and the obedience of faith. The Church chose it for this Sunday because it speaks of a secret kept for ages and revealed now, just as Mary is about to hear.
str: v. 25a: to God who is able to strengthen you.
vv. 25b–26: the mystery: once hidden, now disclosed, made known to all nations.
v. 27: to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory.
kw: In Paul not a puzzle that no one can solve, but God's plan, hidden until the time he chooses to reveal it (compare Ephesians 3:3–9; Colossians 1:26). Its content is Christ himself and the salvation of all.
The public announcement, as by a herald. The word that strengthens us is not a human idea but a message given and handed on.

The same phrase as Romans 1:5, so the letter begins and ends on it. It is faith that listens and gives itself. The word for “obedience” has the verb “to hear” in it. The Catechism defines the phrase in CCC 143–144.
vv: according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages

A note on the text. Manuscripts place this doxology at different points in Romans, in some after 14:23 or 15:33, and a few omit it, so scholars debate its origin. It belongs to the canonical text of Scripture as the Church received it, and the Church proclaims it as the word of God.
but is now disclosed, and through the prophetic writings is made known to all the Gentiles
The prophets did not fall silent when Christ came. They became understandable. That is what today's readings are doing: 2 Samuel lights up in the Gospel, and the Gospel is explained by 2 Samuel.
to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever! Amen.
The whole of theology ends in praise. Paul has spent sixteen chapters explaining, and his last word is glory.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this phrase: “the obedience of faith” is to be given to God who reveals, by which we entrust our whole selves to God (Dei Verbum 5). The Catechism says that Mary “most perfectly embodies the obedience of faith” (CCC 148). Paul's general truth stands today beside its most perfect example.

r.h: Let it be with me according to your word
set: Yesterday's Gospel set the angel in the temple, with a priest, at the hour of incense. Today the same angel is sent to a village in Galilee which the Old Testament never mentions, to a girl with no office. Luke invites the comparison. “The sixth month” refers to Elizabeth's pregnancy (1:24, 36). Mary is “engaged” to Joseph: legally bound to him but not yet living with him.
str: vv. 26–27: the setting: Nazareth, a virgin, Joseph of the house of David.
vv. 28–29: the greeting, and Mary's reflection.
vv. 30–33: the announcement, in the words of 2 Samuel 7.
v. 34: Mary's question.
vv. 35–37: the answer: the Spirit, the overshadowing; Elizabeth as a sign.
v. 38: Mary's consent.
kw: The usual Greek greeting, but its root meaning is “rejoice”, and the Greek Old Testament uses the same word in calling Daughter Zion to joy (Zephaniah 3:14; Zechariah 9:9). The Catechism hears this echo (CCC 722, 2676).

A perfect passive participle of charitoō, “to fill with favour”: one who has been and remains graced by God. It stands in the place of her name. The Latin Vulgate's gratia plena, “full of grace”, gave the Church the words of the Hail Mary.

The word of Exodus 40:35 in the Greek Old Testament, where the cloud settled on the tent of meeting and God's glory filled it. It returns at the Transfiguration (Luke 9:34). Mary becomes the place where God dwells.

The feminine of the word for slave or servant. It is the title of Abraham, Moses and David in the Scriptures (compare 2 Samuel 7:5: “my servant David”). It is not servility but a title of honour and of total belonging.
An optative, the Greek mood of wishing. It is more than resigned acceptance; it has desire in it.
vv: And he came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.”

God's promise to be with someone is the word given to those called to a great task, like Moses, Gideon or Jeremiah (Exodus 3:12; Judges 6:12; Jeremiah 1:8). Here there is more: the Lord will be with her in a way that has never been true of anyone.
He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David.
Read beside today's first reading: great name, son, throne. Each is taken from Nathan's oracle. All of Israel's waiting comes down to this one sentence, spoken quietly in a village.
He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.
The Creed of the Church takes up these words: “and his kingdom will have no end”.
Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?”
Literally, “since I do not know a man”, which is what the POC renders. See the question below.
The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God.

The Trinity is present in one verse: the Spirit, the Most High, and the Son. A new creation begins with the Spirit, whom the Fathers saw moving over the first one (Genesis 1:2), and no human father is involved. The “throne of David” has now become something no one could have imagined: David's heir is Son of God.
For nothing will be impossible with God.

An echo of what was said to Sarah: “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” (Genesis 18:14). In Greek rhēma means both “word” and “thing”: no word of God will fail. Then Mary replies in the same term: “according to your word”.
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
“Here am I” is the reply of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah. Mary's reply is the turning point of history, given in the name of all. God does not force his way in; he asks.
ch: The Catechism teaches that “full of grace” expresses Mary's being redeemed from the moment of her conception (CCC 490–492), and that by her consent she “becomes the mother of Jesus” (CCC 494). It quotes St Irenaeus: the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by Mary's obedience (CCC 494; Lumen Gentium 56). The Council says that the Fathers rightly see Mary not as a merely passive instrument but as cooperating by her faith and obedience (Lumen Gentium 56). St Augustine says that she conceived Christ in her heart by faith before she conceived him in her womb (in substance; see CCC 506). St Bernard, in a homily well known from the Office of Readings, pictures the whole world waiting for her reply (in substance). The Catechism adds that the angel's words give the Church her Hail Mary (CCC 2676): in Mary, “the daughter of Zion in person”, the ark of the covenant has found its fulfillment.

qa: Did God's promise fail when David's kingdom ended in 587 BC?

That was the pain of Psalm 89, which sings the promise and then laments that the crown is in the dust (Psalm 89:38–39). For centuries there was no king. But the prophets kept the promise alive (Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), and Gabriel announces its fulfillment. The promise did not fail. It was fulfilled in a way that goes beyond any earthly throne: Christ's kingdom “will have no end”.
Why did Mary ask how, if she was already engaged to Joseph?

An engaged young woman might simply expect a child within her marriage. St Augustine, and many after him, saw in her words a resolve to remain a virgin (in substance). Other Catholic scholars read the question as Luke's way of leading the story to the angel's great answer in v. 35. The Church has not defined how the question is to be explained. What is clear in the text is that Mary does not doubt, that she asks how, and that she gives her consent.
Why do Catholics say “full of grace” if the NRSV has “favored one”?

Both translate kecharitōmenē. “Favored one” is the plainer rendering; “full of grace” (gratia plena) is the older Latin one, and it brings out the perfect tense: a favour already given and still lasting. The Church's teaching on Mary's holiness does not rest on one word alone, but the greeting is one of its main scriptural roots (CCC 490–491).
rite: In the Roman Rite this is the last Sunday of Advent, and the fourth candle of the wreath is lit in many parishes. The Mass today gathers up the whole season: the Entrance Antiphon is Rorate caeli (Isaiah 45:8), the prayer of the Collect is the one Catholics know from the end of the Angelus, “Pour forth, we beseech you, O Lord, your grace into our hearts”, and this evening's O Antiphon is O Clavis David, “O Key of David”, which fits a day given over to the promise made to David. A fitting family practice for today is to pray the Angelus together: the Gospel of the Mass is the prayer itself.
study: David wanted to build something for God, and God answered by building something for David. Where am I trying to do things for God, without first receiving what he is doing for me?
What is the “mystery kept secret” that the Scriptures have made clear to me? How has the Old Testament helped me to understand Christ?
Mary asks a real question before she consents. How does this help me to bring my questions to God honestly?
What would it mean for my home to become a “house” where Christ can be born this Christmas? What one “yes” is God asking of me?

lead: With Christmas four days away, the Church lets the Scripture of love speak. The beloved comes “leaping upon the mountains”, and in the Gospel Mary hurries through the hill country and the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps for joy. The alternative first reading, from Zephaniah, calls Daughter Zion to rejoice because the Lord is in her midst. Psalm 33 tells the just to exult. All three say that the Lord is near, and that the proper response is joy.

r.h: The voice of my beloved
set: “The Song of Songs” is a Hebrew way of saying the greatest of songs. It is a collection of love poems between a woman and a man, and it barely mentions God at all. Yet Jewish tradition read it as the love of God and Israel, and Rabbi Akiba called it the holy of holies among the Scriptures (Mishnah, Yadayim 3:5). Christian tradition, in Origen, St Gregory of Nyssa and St Bernard, read it as the love of Christ and the Church, and of Christ and the soul. Here the woman tells what she heard at the end of winter.
str: vv. 8–9: she hears him and sees him: he is coming, he is at the wall.
vv. 10–13: his call: “Arise”; winter is over, spring has come.
v. 14: he asks to see her face and hear her voice.
kw: Her name for him throughout the poem, a word of tender intimacy. It opens the passage: the first thing is his voice.
Literally “arise for yourself” and then “go for yourself”. The same call frames vv. 10 and 13. Love does not drag; it calls.
A tender name in love poetry. The dove is shy, hidden in the rock. He asks her to come out of hiding.
vv: The voice of my beloved! Look, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.

No obstacle stops him. St Gregory the Great applied the “leaps” to Christ: from heaven to the womb, from the womb to the manger, from the manger to the Cross, from the Cross to the tomb, and from the tomb to heaven (in substance).
for now the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.

In the land of Israel the winter rains end in spring, and the hills flower. The Church reads this in the dark of December (in the northern hemisphere) as a promise: the long winter of waiting is nearly over.
let me see your face, let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.
He seeks her as much as she seeks him. In the Christian reading it is God who desires to hear our voice. Today's Gospel gives that voice: Mary's greeting.
ch: The Catechism says that Tradition has always seen in the Song of Solomon a unique expression of human love, a reflection of God's own love, “strong as death” (CCC 1611). Both senses matter. It honours the love of husband and wife, and it teaches the Church to hear Christ as the Bridegroom (CCC 796). Placed before the Visitation, it invites us to hear Mary's journey as the beloved's coming, for she carries him.

r.h: The Lord is in your midst
set: This is the other option the lectionary gives for today's first reading. After the judgment on Jerusalem and the promise of a humble remnant (read last Tuesday), the book of Zephaniah ends with joy. Zion is called to sing, for the Lord has cancelled the sentence against her.
str: v. 14: the call to rejoice.
v. 15: why: the judgment is lifted; the King is here.
vv. 16–18a: do not fear: God himself rejoices over you.
kw: Jerusalem and her people pictured as a woman. The Catechism sees Mary as “the daughter of Zion in person” (CCC 2676).
Twice here (vv. 15, 17). The Hebrew word can also mean “within you”, “in your inner part”. Some Catholic scholars hear in it a link with the Annunciation; this is a suggestion, not a settled reading.
vv: Sing aloud, O daughter Zion; shout, O Israel!
The Greek Old Testament begins this verse with chaire, “rejoice”, the very word of Gabriel to Mary (Luke 1:28).
The king of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst; you shall fear disaster no more.
The Malayalam POC numbers these words as v. 16.
he will rejoice over you with gladness, he will renew you in his love; he will exult over you with loud singing

A note on the text. “He will renew you” follows the Greek and Syriac; the Hebrew reads “he will be silent in his love”. Each is beautiful. It is rare in the Bible and most moving to hear of God singing for joy over his people.
ch: The Catechism quotes these words when it explains the Hail Mary: “Rejoice ... O Daughter of Jerusalem ... the Lord your God is in your midst” (CCC 2676), and it says that Gabriel rightly greets Mary as Daughter of Zion (CCC 722).

r.h: Blessed is she who believed
set: Mary has just given her consent, and Gabriel has told her of Elizabeth (1:36). She goes at once. The “Judean town in the hill country” is not named; an old tradition places it at Ein Karem, west of Jerusalem. Two women meet here with no man in the scene, and both carry a child whom God has promised.
str: v. 39: Mary goes in haste.
vv. 40–41: the greeting: the child leaps, and Elizabeth is filled with the Spirit.
vv. 42–45: Elizabeth's cry, in three parts: blessed are you; why me?; blessed is she who believed.
kw: A vivid word. The Greek Old Testament uses it of the twins struggling in Rebekah's womb (Genesis 25:22). Here it is “for joy” (v. 44). John is doing his work as forerunner before he is born.
“Blessed are you among women” echoes the praise of Judith (Judith 13:18). The next line, “blessed is the fruit of your womb”, has passed into the Hail Mary.
A different Greek word in v. 45, the word of the Beatitudes. Elizabeth gives the first beatitude of Luke's Gospel, to Mary, and for her faith.
vv: When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit
Luke does not record what Mary says, only its effect. Her voice carries the presence of her Son, and the Spirit comes with him.
And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?

Many commentators hear David's words before the ark: “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9). David danced before the ark, and the ark stayed three months in a house that was blessed (2 Samuel 6:11, 14); John leaps, and Mary stays about three months (Luke 1:56). “Lord” is the title Luke has been using for God all through this chapter (1:6, 9, 11), and Elizabeth uses it of the unborn child. The Church's title “Mother of God” has its root here (CCC 495).
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.
Zechariah did not believe (1:20); Mary did. Elizabeth, Zechariah's wife, says this with no bitterness at all. It is the first beatitude in Luke, and Mary's greatness lies here.
ch: The Catechism sees the Visitation as God's visit to his people: John is filled with the Spirit by Christ, whom Mary has just conceived (CCC 717). It says that Mary “most perfectly embodies the obedience of faith” and that for this faith all generations call her blessed (CCC 148). St John Paul II takes Elizabeth's words as the key to Mary's whole life in Redemptoris Mater (1987), nn. 12–19. St Ambrose, whose words on this Gospel are read in today's Office of Readings, says: let the soul of Mary be in each one, to magnify the Lord (in substance).

qa: Why does Mary go “with haste”?

Luke does not give a reason in so many words, and the text does not say that she went to check the angel's sign. Everything suggests joy and love: she has a relative in need and news to share. St Ambrose says that the grace of the Holy Spirit knows nothing of slow efforts (in substance). The Christ whom she carries sets her at once on the road to someone else.
rite: Today's O Antiphon is O Oriens, “O Dayspring” or “O Rising Dawn”, sung near the shortest day of the northern year: splendour of eternal light and sun of justice. It recalls Zechariah's song: “the dawn from on high will break upon us” (Luke 1:78). Today is also the optional memorial of St Peter Canisius, priest and doctor.
study: Mary's first act after receiving Christ is to go to someone in need. To whom should I go before Christmas?
“Blessed is she who believed.” Which of God's promises do I find hardest to trust at this moment?

lead: Two mothers sing today, a thousand years apart. Hannah brings the child she begged from God and gives him back. Mary, carrying the child she did not ask for, sings a song full of Hannah's words. The psalm response today is Hannah's own canticle, so the three texts form one hymn: God looks on the lowly, and those who receive everything from him give everything back.

r.h: For this child I prayed
set: Israel is still in the time of the judges, with no king, and the ark is kept at the sanctuary of Shiloh under the priest Eli. Hannah had no child and was mocked for it. She prayed in tears and vowed that a son would be given back to the Lord (1:11). When Samuel was born she stayed at home until he was weaned (1:22). In the ancient world a child might be nursed for about three years (compare 2 Maccabees 7:27).
str: v. 24: Hannah goes up to Shiloh with the child and her offerings.
v. 25: the sacrifice; the child is brought to Eli.
vv. 26–28: Hannah speaks: I am the woman who prayed here; the Lord answered; now I give him back.
kw: The key verb of the chapter. Hannah explains Samuel's name with it: “I have asked him of the Lord” (1:20). In v. 27 she uses it for her petition, and in v. 28 a form of the same verb gives “lent”, “given”. What she asked of God she now hands back to God.
Her name means grace or favour. The whole story is about favour received by someone who had no claim to it.
vv: For this child I prayed; and the Lord has granted me the petition that I made to him.
Eli had once taken her for a drunken woman (1:13–14). Now she stands in the same place with the living answer in her arms.
Therefore I have lent him to the Lord; as long as he lives, he is given to the Lord.

She gives away the only thing she ever asked for. A note on the text: at two points the ancient witnesses differ. NRSV and POC have “a three-year-old bull” in v. 24, while the standard Hebrew text has “three bulls”. At the end of v. 28 NRSV says “She left him there”, while POC says that they worshipped the Lord.
ch: The Catechism names Hannah, the mother of Samuel, among the holy women through whom God prepared the mission of Mary, choosing those who were considered powerless and weak to show his faithfulness (CCC 489). The Church hears in her gift the pattern of every parent who brings a child to God, and of Mary, who will carry her own son to the Temple and offer him there (Luke 2:22).

r.h: The Mighty One has done great things for me
set: Mary has gone in haste to the hill country and Elizabeth has called her blessed (1:42–45). Her answer is the Magnificat, named after its first word in Latin. It is woven from the Old Testament, above all the song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10). Luke ends with Mary's return home, closing her part of the scene before he tells of John's birth.
str: vv. 46–49: Mary's own praise: God has looked on her lowliness.
v. 50: his mercy from generation to generation.
vv. 51–53: the great reversal: the proud and the powerful, the lowly and the hungry.
vv. 54–55: God remembers his promise to Israel and to Abraham.
v. 56: Mary stays about three months and returns home.
kw: To declare someone great. Mary does not make God greater; she makes his greatness known. In Latin the word is magnificat.
A low, humbled condition, not only a modest attitude. In the Greek Old Testament Hannah prays with the same word: “if only you will look on the misery of your servant” (1 Samuel 1:11).
A title of God in the Old Testament, the warrior who saves (compare Zephaniah 3:17). His power shows itself here in a young woman's pregnancy.
vv: My soul magnifies the Lord,
A note on the text: nearly all manuscripts name Mary as the singer. A very few Old Latin witnesses have “Elizabeth”. The Church reads the song as Mary's.
for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
This is the biblical root of devotion to Mary. She is called blessed because of what God has done for her, and she says so herself.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly;
The verbs are in the past tense, though the world looks unchanged. Mary sings of God's coming victory as already won, because it has begun in her womb.
ch: St Ambrose, commenting on Luke, says that the soul of Mary should be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each of us to rejoice in God (in substance). The Church sings the Magnificat every evening at Evening Prayer; the Catechism calls it the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church (CCC 2619). On the honour paid to Mary, see CCC 971. St John Paul II taught that the Church's love of preference for the poor is written into the Magnificat (Redemptoris Mater 37, in substance).

qa: Do these words of Mary speak against the rich?

They warn against pride and against wealth that shuts out God and neighbour, as the words “in the thoughts of their hearts” (1:51) suggest. They do not condemn a person for owning something. Their promise is that God sees those whom the world overlooks.
rite: From 17 to 23 December the Latin Church sings a special antiphon with the Magnificat at Evening Prayer, each beginning with “O”. Today's is O Rex gentium, O King of the nations. The Gospel's song is thus framed each evening by the longing for the coming King.
study: Hannah gave back what she had most wanted. What gift of God am I still holding too tightly?
Mary praises God for what he has done before she speaks of what she needs. How would my daily prayer change if it began in the same way?

lead: Two days before Christmas the Church reads the end of the last prophet of the Book of the Twelve and the birth of the man who fulfils his words. Malachi promises a messenger and the return of Elijah. Luke shows the messenger's first days: a child is named, a silent father speaks, and the whole hill country asks who this child will be.

r.h: I am sending my messenger
