set: Malachi speaks after the exile, probably in the fifth century BC. The Temple has been rebuilt, but worship has become careless and people ask, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17). Today's reading answers: the Lord himself is coming, and his coming will purify.

A note on numbering: the Hebrew text of Malachi has three chapters, and the Lectionary follows it. The NRSV and the POC print the last verses as chapter 4, so 3:23–24 is the same as 4:5–6 in the quotations below. In many Christian Bibles these are the last verses of the Old Testament.
str: 3:1: the messenger, and the Lord who comes to his Temple.
3:2–3: the fire and the soap: he purifies the descendants of Levi.
3:4: worship pleasing to the Lord again.
4:5–6 (Lectionary 3:23–24): Elijah before the day of the Lord.
kw: The same word gives the book its name. It may be a personal name or a title. Mal’āk means an envoy, human or angelic. The same verse also speaks of “the messenger of the covenant”.
The fuller's lye, used to clean cloth. With the refiner's fire it makes two ordinary images of trades that clean by burning and by beating. God's coming is good news, but it is not comfortable.
vv: See, I am sending my messenger to prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.

The Gospels apply this verse to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27). Once John has prepared the way, the Lord comes to his Temple: Luke will show the child Jesus carried there (2:22).
But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap;
Fire burns away what is false, but it is used on what is precious. A refiner does not throw away silver.
Lo, I will send you the prophet Elijah before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.
Elijah did not die but was taken up (2 Kings 2:11), so Israel looked for his return. Jewish custom still keeps that hope alive at the Passover table.
He will turn the hearts of parents to their children and the hearts of children to their parents,

Before the great day comes, homes must be healed. The book's last word is “curse”; when Jewish readers read it aloud they repeat the previous verse, so as not to end there. The angel takes up this verse when he tells Zechariah about John (Luke 1:17).
ch: Jesus says of John, “he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14). The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate precursor, going before him “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (CCC 523; see 718–719). Early Christians also heard in Malachi a promise of pure worship: the Didache applies Malachi 1:11 to the Eucharist, and the Roman Eucharistic Prayer III echoes that verse in the words “from the rising of the sun to its setting”.

r.h: His name is John
set: Nine months earlier the angel had told Zechariah in the Temple that Elizabeth would bear a son and that he must be called John (1:13). Zechariah doubted and was struck silent (1:20). Now the word comes true. On the eighth day, as the Law commands (Leviticus 12:3), the family gathers for the circumcision.
str: vv. 57–58: the birth, and the neighbours' joy at God's mercy.
vv. 59–61: the dispute about the name.
vv. 62–63: Zechariah writes: “His name is John.”
v. 64: his mouth is opened and he praises God.
vv. 65–66: fear and wonder spread through the hill country.
kw: The Hebrew name means “the Lord has been gracious”. None of the relatives has this name (1:61): the child's name comes from God, not from family custom.
In 1:58 Luke uses the same verb as Mary's “magnifies” (1:46): literally, the Lord “magnified” his mercy to Elizabeth.
An Old Testament expression for God's power at work in a person. Luke's comment closes the scene and looks ahead to John's mission.
vv: But his mother said, “No; he is to be called John.”
Luke does not tell us how she knew. Zechariah could have written it for her, or the Spirit could have shown her. What matters is that the mother speaks up first, against all custom.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And all of them were amazed.

He does not write “let his name be” but “his name is”. The name has already been given by God. Zechariah's obedience is the moment his silence ends. The relatives had to make signs to him (1:62), which suggests that he could not hear either.
“What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.
This is the Advent question. It is asked of every child brought to the font.
ch: The Catechism says that when the Church celebrates the precursor's birth and martyrdom she unites herself to his desire: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (CCC 524; John 3:30). The Latin calendar keeps the birthdays of only three persons: Jesus, Mary and John. St Augustine, preaching on the Baptist, calls John the voice and Christ the Word; and he notes that John was born when the days begin to shorten and Christ when they begin to lengthen (in substance).

rite: Tonight's antiphon at Evening Prayer is the last of the series: O Emmanuel, God with us (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). The Latin titles of the seven antiphons, read from last to first, begin with letters that spell Ero cras, “I will be there tomorrow”. Whether this was intended is not certain, but many have loved the thought.
study: Malachi says the Lord comes as a refiner. What in my life do I hope he will burn away by Christmas?
Zechariah's first words after nine months are praise. What has my own silence or difficulty taught me to say to God?

lead: This morning is the last of Advent. David wants to build God a house, and God answers that he will build David a house instead. In the Gospel an old priest, his voice just restored, sings that the promise has come: God “has raised up a mighty savior for us in the house of his servant David”. A thousand years of waiting end in one sentence, and at evening the Church begins Christmas.

r.h: The Lord will make you a house
set: David has taken Jerusalem and brought the ark there (2 Samuel 5–6). The wars are quiet and he lives in a cedar palace. It seems only right that God should have a house too, and the prophet Nathan at first agrees. This chapter, the oracle of Nathan, is one of the foundations of Israel's hope for the Messiah. It is echoed in Psalm 89, today's psalm.
str: vv. 1–3: David's plan; Nathan's first yes.
vv. 4–5: that night God speaks: “Are you the one?”
vv. 8b–9: I took you from the sheep; I have been with you.
vv. 10–11: a place for Israel, rest, and the promise of a house.
v. 12: your offspring and his kingdom.
vv. 14a, 16: father and son; a house and a throne forever.
kw: The whole oracle turns on this word. It means a building (a palace, a temple) and also a family line. David offers a building; God promises a dynasty.
Literally seed. In the first place it is Solomon, who will build the Temple (7:13; 1 Kings 6). But “forever” goes beyond any one son.
The word comes back in vv. 13 and 16. The kings of David's line fell and the throne stood empty after the exile, but Israel did not stop hoping.
vv: See now, I am living in a house of cedar, but the ark of God stays in a tent.
A generous thought. Yet the story shows that even a good plan for God can be our plan and not his.
Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
God is not refusing honour. He is reversing the direction: grace always begins from God's side.
Moreover the Lord declares to you that the Lord will make you a house.
This is the turning point of the chapter. The man who wanted to give receives.
Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me; your throne shall be established forever.
A note on the text: the standard Hebrew text has “before you”; NRSV and POC read “before me”, with the Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts.
ch: The New Testament reads this oracle of Jesus. Gabriel promises Mary that God will give her son “the throne of his ancestor David”, and “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33), words the Creed repeats. Hebrews 1:5, heard at tomorrow's Mass, applies 7:14 to the Son. The Catechism presents Jesus as the messianic Son of David (CCC 439) and notes that the Temple David wished to build was the work of his son (CCC 2580).

r.h: The dawn from on high will break upon us
set: Zechariah's mouth has just been opened (1:64). Filled with the Holy Spirit, he speaks the song the Church calls the Benedictus, from its first word in Latin. Like the Magnificat, it is made of Old Testament language. It has the form of a Jewish blessing of God for his saving acts. A priest of the old covenant here stands at the door of the new.
str: vv. 67–75: God blessed for what he has done: the savior from David's house, the mercy to the ancestors, the oath to Abraham, so that we may serve him without fear.
vv. 76–77: to the child: you will go before the Lord.
vv. 78–79: the dawn from on high, light in darkness, the way of peace.
kw: Used at the opening (1:68) and the close (1:78). In the Old Testament God “visits” his people to save them (Exodus 4:31).

The word for the rising of the sun or a star. The Greek Old Testament also uses it for the messianic “Branch” (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8). Latin renders it Oriens, the title in the antiphon of 21 December. Compare Malachi 4:2, “the sun of righteousness shall rise”.
The name means “the Lord remembers”. In v. 72 the song says that God “has remembered his holy covenant”.
vv: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked favorably on his people and redeemed them.
Jesus has not been born yet, but Zechariah speaks in the past tense. For faith, God's promise is as sure as what has been done.
And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways,
An eight-day-old infant receives his life's task. “The Most High” is the title given to Jesus' Father in 1:32; in Luke “the Lord” also points to Jesus (1:43).
By the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will break upon us,

A note on the text: the manuscripts vary between “will break” (which NRSV and POC follow) and “has broken”. Literally “tender mercy” is the “bowels of mercy”, the deep feeling of God. The whole salvation comes out of this.
ch: The Church sings the Benedictus each morning at Morning Prayer, so each day begins with the promise that the dawn is coming. The Catechism calls John “Prophet of the Most High”, the last of the prophets, who goes before Jesus (CCC 523), and says that in him the Holy Spirit concludes his speaking through the prophets (CCC 719).

qa: If God promised a throne forever, what happened when David's line stopped ruling?

The Church's answer is that the promise was greater than a political kingdom. Jesus reigns as the risen Son of David, and his kingdom has no end (Luke 1:33; CCC 439). The Jewish people's long hope for God's anointed is honoured by the Church as part of the same story (CCC 839–840).
rite: This Mass is the last of Advent, in violet, with its own readings. From the evening the Mass of the Vigil of Christmas begins, with the Gospel of the genealogy of Jesus. The title Oriens and the song of Zechariah join here: the dawn this song awaits comes with Christmas.
study: David wanted to build for God, and God wanted to build for David. Where is my plan for God standing in the way of God's plan for me?
“To guide our feet into the way of peace”: where is my family or parish most in need of that way this Christmas?

lead: The Mass during the Day does not retell the story of Bethlehem. Luke's shepherds and manger belong to the Masses of the night and of dawn. Now, in full daylight, the Church asks who this child is.

The three readings give one answer in three voices. Isaiah sees a messenger running over the mountains with the news that God has come back to his ruined city. Hebrews says that the God who spoke in fragments through the prophets has now spoken by a Son, the very imprint of his being. John goes back behind creation itself: “In the beginning was the Word”, and ends with the sentence on which all Christian faith rests: “the Word became flesh”. The key words are messenger, Son and Word.

r.h: Your God reigns
set: This passage belongs to the Book of Consolation (Isaiah 40–55), which speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon in the years before Cyrus allowed them to return (539 BC). Jerusalem lies in ruins. Chapter 52 opens with a call to the city to wake up and rise from the dust (52:1–2).

The poet imagines the day of return as a scene. Watchmen stand on the broken walls. A runner appears on the mountains. Before anyone can see the returning exiles, they hear the news that the Lord himself is coming home at their head. Directly after this passage comes the song of the Suffering Servant (52:13–53:12), which asks, “to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (53:1).
str: v. 7: the messenger on the mountains.
v. 8: the sentinels see the Lord's return.
v. 9: the ruins themselves are told to sing.
v. 10: the Lord's arm, and salvation for all the earth.
kw: One who brings good news, especially news of victory. The Greek Old Testament uses a verb from the same family as euangelion, “gospel”. This is one of the roots of the Christian word.
The whole message in two Hebrew words. It is the Lord, not Babylon, who is king. The Gospel opens with the same news: “the kingdom of God has come near” (Mark 1:15).
God's arm is his saving power, the arm that brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 6:6). To bare it is to roll back the sleeve and go to work.
From the same root as the name Yeshua, Jesus. On this day the word has a new sound.
vv: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns.”

Feet are not usually called beautiful, least of all feet that have run over mountain paths. They are beautiful because of what they bring. St Paul quotes this verse of those who preach Christ (Romans 10:15).
Listen! Your sentinels lift up their voices, together they sing for joy; for in plain sight they see the return of the Lord to Zion.
“In plain sight” is literally “eye to eye”. The glory that left the Temple (Ezekiel 10) returns, and it can be seen. John will say, “we have seen his glory”.
Break forth together into singing, you ruins of Jerusalem;
It is the ruins who are told to sing, before any stone has been rebuilt. Comfort has come already, because God has come.
The Lord has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.
The news is not only for Israel. The psalm today answers in the past tense: all the ends of the earth have seen it (Psalm 98:3).
ch: The Church hears in this messenger first of all Christ, who “came and proclaimed peace” (Ephesians 2:17), and then everyone who carries him to others. St Paul VI taught that evangelizing is the grace and vocation proper to the Church, her deepest identity (Evangelii Nuntiandi 14). So the messenger's feet are the feet of every catechist and parent who hands on this news.

r.h: God has spoken by a Son
set: Hebrews calls itself “a word of exhortation” (13:22). It is a sermon to Christians who were growing weary. Its author is not named. These opening verses are among the finest Greek of the New Testament, and they state the theme of the whole work: Christ is God's final word and the one true high priest.

Our reading ends at v. 6, in the middle of a chain of Old Testament quotations (1:5–14) showing that the Son is greater than the angels. Many Jews of the time held that the Law had been delivered through angels (compare Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2), so the comparison is a way of saying that the Son stands above every messenger who has gone before.
str: vv. 1–2a: two ways of God's speaking: long ago by the prophets, now by a Son.
vv. 2b–3: seven statements about the Son: heir, agent of creation, reflection of glory, imprint of being, sustainer of all things, purifier from sin, seated at the right hand.
v. 4: superior to the angels.
vv. 5–6: the proof from Scripture: Psalm 2:7, 2 Samuel 7:14, and a text calling the angels to worship.
kw: Literally in many parts and many manners. Each prophet gave a part, and truly. The Son is the whole.
The light that shines out from a source. The Book of Wisdom uses this word of Wisdom (Wisdom 7:26). The radiance is not a second light; it has the same nature as its source.
The mark a seal or die leaves on wax or a coin, the exact likeness of the original. Our word “character” comes from it.
God's own reality. Later theology used this word for the divine Persons, but here it has the older sense of essential being.
A title of rank and inheritance (Psalm 89:27), not a claim that the Son was created. It is the same Psalm 89 heard at yesterday's Mass.
vv: Long ago God spoke to our ancestors in many and various ways by the prophets,
The old revelation was true and came from God. The author does not despise it; he calls it God's speech. It was unfinished, not false.
but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son,
The Greek has no article, literally “in Son”: the point is the kind of messenger. God has no further word to add to this one.
He is the reflection of God’s glory and the exact imprint of God’s very being,
Two images side by side, because each alone could mislead. Light and its radiance show that they cannot be separated; a seal and its imprint show that they are distinct.
When he had made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,
Already, in the Christmas reading, the Cross and the Ascension. The priests of old stood at their work; this one sits, because the work is finished (10:11–12). The words recall Psalm 110:1.
“Let all God’s angels worship him.”

The wording is close to the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 32:43 (compare Psalm 97:7); the standard Hebrew of Deuteronomy does not have this line. “When he brings the firstborn into the world” has been read of the Incarnation and also of Christ's return in glory. On this day the angels' song at Bethlehem (Luke 2:13–14) comes to mind.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses to teach that Christ is God's one and final Word, and it adds the words of St John of the Cross: in giving us his Son, his only Word, God spoke everything to us at once, and he has no more to say (CCC 65). There will be no new public revelation before the Lord's return in glory (CCC 66). The Catechism also cites Hebrews 1:3 among the texts confessing the divinity of the Son (CCC 241).

St Athanasius used “reflection of God's glory” against the Arians: since a light is never without its radiance, the Father has never been without the Son (in substance). It is the thought behind “Light from Light” in the Creed.

r.h: The Word became flesh
set: The Prologue stands over the whole Fourth Gospel like a title. It opens with the same words as the Greek Book of Genesis: en archē, “in the beginning”. Mark begins with John at the Jordan, Matthew and Luke with the birth; John begins in eternity.

Behind the term “Word” are two lines of the Old Testament: the word of God that creates (“God said”, Genesis 1) and speaks through the prophets, and Wisdom, who is with God from the beginning and pitches her tent in Israel (Proverbs 8:22–31; Sirach 24:8). Greek readers also knew logos as the reason behind the universe. John takes up all of this and says something none of it had said: this Word has a human name.
str: vv. 1–5: the Word with God, in creation, and as life and light.
vv. 6–8: John, a witness to the light.
vv. 9–13: the light comes into the world; some refuse, some receive and become children of God.
v. 14: the Word became flesh.
v. 15: John's witness again.
vv. 16–18: grace upon grace; the only Son has made God known.

¶ The shorter form leaves out the verses on the Baptist and the last verses. The movement of the whole is a descent and a return: from the Father's side (v. 1) to our flesh (v. 14), and back to “the Father's heart” (v. 18).
kw: Speech, reason, meaning. In Hebrew thought dābār is a word that does what it says. The Word is God's self-expression, a Person (“he”), not a mere message.
The Greek preposition suggests being turned toward God, a relationship. From the first verse the Word is distinct from the Father and yet God.
Not only a body, but human nature in its weakness and mortality. John chooses the strongest word. In his day some could not accept that God would touch flesh (compare 1 John 4:2).
Literally “pitched his tent”. The word recalls the tent in the desert, where the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34), and Wisdom's tent (Sirach 24:8).
These likely echo the great pair of Exodus 34:6, God's ḥesed and ’ĕmet, “steadfast love and faithfulness”, the self-description of God given to Moses.
vv: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
“Was”, three times: not “came to be”. Nothing here has a start. The last clause has no article before “God” in Greek, so it does not say that the Word is the Father, but that the Word is what God is.
in him was life, and the life was the light of all people.
A note on the text: the old manuscripts have no punctuation, so “what has come into being” may close v. 3 or open v. 4. NRSV takes the second course, POC the first. Both are ancient.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
The verb can mean both “overcome” and “grasp”: the darkness neither understood the light nor put it out. The tense of “shines” is the present. This is still happening.
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not accept him.

This is not a verdict on the Jewish people: the first who accepted him, Mary, Joseph, John and the apostles, were Jews, and the Church rejects any blame laid on the Jews as a people (Nostra Aetate 4). It describes every heart that closes its door, ours included.
But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave power to become children of God,

The Son of God by nature makes children of God by grace. A note on v. 13: all Greek manuscripts have the plural “who were born”. A few early Latin witnesses, with Irenaeus and Tertullian, have a singular “who was born”, which would refer to Christ.
And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father’s only son, full of grace and truth.
Not “seemed to be” and not “was changed into”. He remained God and became man. In the desert the glory filled a tent; now it is seen in a man's face. “We have seen”: this is the voice of witnesses.
From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.
No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known.

A note on the text: the oldest manuscripts read “only God” or “God the only one”, others “the only Son”. NRSV combines them, and POC also says that the only-begotten is God himself. “Made him known” (Greek exēgēsato) gives us our word “exegesis”: Jesus is the Father's own exegesis.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Word became flesh to save us, so that we might know God's love, to be our model of holiness, and to make us “partakers of the divine nature” (CCC 456–460). It cites St Athanasius: the Son of God became man so that we might become God (CCC 460). The Incarnation does not mean that Jesus is partly God and partly man, nor a mixture: he is truly God and truly man (CCC 464).

St Augustine says in his Confessions that he found in the books of the Platonists something like “the Word was God”, but not “the Word became flesh” (in substance). St Leo the Great, in a Christmas sermon, tells the Christian to recognize his dignity, now that he shares in God's own nature (CCC 1691). The Church turns this verse into daily prayer in the Angelus.

qa: Was Jesus really born on 25 December?

The Gospels do not give the date. The Church's oldest clear witness to the feast on this day is a Roman calendar in a collection of the year 354. Scholars still debate why this day was chosen: some link it with a Roman festival of the sun, others with an old calculation from 25 March. What the Church celebrates is the fact of the birth, not an exact date in the calendar. On the mystery of Christmas, see CCC 525–526.
“The Word was God”: some translate it “a god”. Is that right?

No. In Greek, a noun placed before the verb without an article commonly describes what someone is, here God's own nature. The Prologue also says that all things were made through him (1:3), which excludes his being a creature. The Council of Nicaea (325) confessed him “true God from true God”. And since the Word is “with God”, he is not the Father: the divine Persons are really distinct (CCC 253–254).
If God has said everything in his Son, why do we still need the Church's teaching?

Revelation is complete, but “it has not been made completely explicit; it remains for Christian faith gradually to grasp its full significance over the course of the centuries” (CCC 66). The Church does not add to it; she goes on understanding and handing it on.
rite: The Latin Church has four Masses of Christmas with their own readings: the Vigil, the Mass during the Night, at Dawn, and during the Day. These are the readings of the last, and they are the same every year. At the Creed today all genuflect at the words “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man”, as also on the Annunciation (General Instruction of the Roman Missal 137). On other days we bow.

For centuries before the reform after the Council, the Prologue was read at the end of nearly every Roman Mass, and all genuflected at “the Word became flesh”. Today the Church hears it on this day above all. The liturgy calls this feast a wonderful exchange: the Creator becomes man, and we are made sharers in his divinity (CCC 526).
study: Isaiah tells the ruins to sing before they have been rebuilt. What ruin in my life or family could begin to sing this Christmas?
Hebrews says God has no further word to add to his Son. Do I look for God's word in him first, or elsewhere?
John says, “his own people did not accept him”. Where do I keep my own door shut against him?
“Grace upon grace”: how can a family tell its children that the crib and the altar hold the same Lord?

lead: The crib is hardly in place when the Church dresses in red. On the day after Christmas she remembers the first to die for the child she has just adored. The feast is not out of place: the Word became flesh so that he could give his life, and Stephen shows what his birth makes possible in a human being. He dies with the words of Jesus on his lips, and he dies forgiving.

Acts shows the promise of the Gospel coming true. Jesus had told his disciples that they would be handed over, and that the Spirit of the Father would speak through them. Stephen argues in the synagogue and stands before the council, and his opponents “could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke”. The reading ends with his prayer: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” The key words are witness and Spirit.

r.h: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit
set: As the Jerusalem community grows, a dispute arises over the care of the Greek-speaking widows. The apostles have seven men chosen, “full of the Spirit and of wisdom” (6:3), and Stephen is named first. He does far more than serve tables: he works wonders and argues in the synagogues of Greek-speaking Jews.

All of this takes place within Judaism. Stephen is a Jew arguing with fellow Jews about the Temple, the Law and the Messiah. He is brought before the council, and in the long speech the reading leaves out (7:2–53) he retells the story of Israel. When he calls his hearers resisters of the Spirit, the anger breaks out. The law against blasphemy prescribed stoning outside the camp (Leviticus 24:14). Scholars debate whether this was a legal sentence or the violence of a crowd; Luke's account reads more like the second.
str: 6:8: Stephen, full of grace and power.
6:9–10: the dispute with the synagogue of the Freedmen, and their defeat.
[6:11–7:53: false witnesses, the charge, the speech (left out of the reading).]
7:54: the rage of the hearers.
7:55–56: Stephen's vision: Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
7:57–58: they rush at him, drive him out and stone him; Saul.
7:59: his prayer to Jesus. (The next verse, his last word of forgiveness, follows the reading.)
kw: A Greek name meaning “crown”, especially the victor's wreath. Tradition has loved the coincidence: the first martyr is the first to be crowned.

In Acts it means one who testifies to what he has seen. Paul will say, “the blood of your witness Stephen was shed” (22:20). From stories like this one, the word “martyr” came to mean one who testifies with his death.
A fixed, intent look (7:55). Luke uses the same word for the apostles looking up at the Ascension (1:10). All around him there is rage; he looks up.
An imperative from dechomai. Jesus on the Cross said to the Father, “into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46); Stephen says the same to Jesus.
vv: Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people.
What Luke said of Jesus (Luke 2:40; 4:14) he now says of a disciple. The life of the Lord is being lived again in his Church.
But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Exactly what Jesus had promised: “a wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to withstand” (Luke 21:15).
But filled with the Holy Spirit, he gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
Psalm 110 and the Creed say that Christ is seated. Why standing? The text does not say. Many have read it as the Lord rising to receive his witness, or to stand as a witness for him.
“Look,” he said, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”

Almost the only time in the New Testament that someone other than Jesus uses the title “Son of Man”. Before this same council Jesus had said that the Son of Man would be seated at God's right hand (Luke 22:69). Stephen reports that it is true.
the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.
A small detail on which the future turned. Saul approves (8:1); he will one day confess it himself (22:20).
While they were stoning Stephen, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”

This is one of the earliest prayers addressed to Jesus. The disciple prays to him as to God, in the moment of death. Luke shapes the story so that the passion of the disciple matches the Passion of the Master: the council, the word about the Son of Man at God's right hand, the giving up of the spirit, the forgiveness of the killers (7:60; Luke 22:69; 23:34, 46).
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom “the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith” (CCC 2473), and Vatican II says that by it the disciple is made like his Master (Lumen Gentium 42). On the forgiveness of enemies, see CCC 2844.

In a sermon read today in the Office of Readings, St Fulgentius of Ruspe says that yesterday our King was born in a robe of flesh, and today his soldier left the tent of the body and went in triumph to heaven; love was Stephen's weapon (in substance). A saying long attributed to St Augustine adds that if Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have Paul. In his City of God Augustine himself tells of healings in Africa through Stephen's relics, which were found in 415 and spread widely.

r.h: The Spirit of your Father speaking through you
set: Chapter 10 of Matthew is the second of Jesus' great discourses, the sending of the Twelve. It begins with the mission to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” and widens to the whole future of the Church. Today's verses look past the first mission to the governors and kings of the Gentile world. Parallel words appear in Mark 13:9–13 and Luke 21:12–19.

When this Gospel was written, Jesus' disciples, most of them Jews, were already living with conflict inside their own synagogues and families, and also with Roman power. These words were not given to stir up hostility toward anyone. They were given to strengthen those who suffered.
str: vv. 17–18: warning: councils, synagogues, governors and kings.
vv. 19–20: promise: do not worry; the Spirit will speak.
v. 21: divided families.
v. 22: hatred, and the promise to the one who endures.
kw: The word used of John the Baptist's arrest (4:12) and of Jesus' own betrayal (26:45). Jesus' disciple goes down the same road.
The courtroom is the place of witness: arrest becomes an opportunity to proclaim Christ. The word is the origin of the word “martyr”.
Literally remaining under a weight. In the New Testament this is not resignation but steadfast, active hope.
vv: Beware of them, for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues;

The Greek says “beware of people” in general (so POC). The warning concerns those who persecute, and it is not aimed at any one nation. Christians and Jews alike have suffered persecution for their faith.
do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say;
This is not a promise for lazy preachers. It is a promise for those standing before a judge.
for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
“The Spirit of your Father” is a rare expression in Matthew. The disciple on trial is a child of the Father, not an orphan.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
“To the end” can mean to the end of a person's life, and to the end of the age. Stephen's end is both a defeat in the world's eyes and the victory the verse promises.
ch: The Catechism lists this passage among the places where Jesus speaks of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit who helps his disciples in the witness they must bear (CCC 728). Service of and witness to the faith are necessary for salvation, it teaches, quoting Lumen Gentium 42 (CCC 1816).
Tertullian wrote in his Apology that the blood of Christians is seed. The Church has seen this in every century, and in our own time.

qa: Why a martyr's feast on the day after Christmas?

It is not a sudden change of mood. The wood of the crib and the wood of the Cross belong together. The feast is very old, and ancient calendars already placed it directly after Christmas. Its meaning is that the same Lord who was born for us gives us the strength to give our lives for him.
Was Stephen a deacon?

Acts does not use the noun “deacon” for the Seven, but the verb “to serve” appears for the work they are chosen to relieve (6:2). St Irenaeus already speaks of Stephen as chosen for the diaconate, and tradition honours him as the first deacon and the patron of deacons. In Acts he also preaches, as the deacons of the Church are called to do (CCC 1570).
Did “the Jews” kill Stephen?

Those who killed him and Stephen himself were all Jews, as were Paul and the first Christians. A group in Jerusalem acted that day; a people did not. The Church teaches that Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, and she deplores all hatred and persecution of them (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
rite: The Mass is in red, the colour of martyrs. It falls within the Octave of Christmas, so the Preface is the Preface of Christmas. Tomorrow is the Sunday of the Holy Family; white returns.

On this day we also remember those who suffer for their faith now. The Latin Church in India has her own witnesses, among them St Devasahayam, the lay martyr of South India canonized in 2022, and we may remember them in the prayer of the faithful.
study: Stephen looked up when everyone around him was raging. Where do I keep my gaze when I am under attack?
Stephen's prayer for his killers came true in Saul. For whom am I being asked to pray, though I may not see the result?
Jesus says, “do not worry about how you are to speak”. When have I been given words at the right moment?
What does it cost me, in my family or at work, to be known as a follower of Christ?

lead: On the Sunday within the Octave of Christmas the Church looks at the home in which the Son of God grew up. In Year B the Lectionary offers these readings, and they begin long before Nazareth, with an old couple who have no child. Abraham and Sarah receive a son only as God's gift. Hebrews shows that Abraham's faith went further: he was ready to give that son back. The psalm sings of the God who remembers his covenant. In Luke, Mary and Joseph carry their child to the Temple, offer him to the Lord, and take him home to grow up. The key words are promise, offering and growing. In each of these households the child is first of all God's gift, not the parents' possession.

r.h: Your heir shall be your own son
set: God had promised Abram a land, a great name and many descendants when he called him out of Haran (Genesis 12:1–4). Years have passed. “After these things” (15:1) points back to chapter 14, where Abram has rescued his nephew Lot from the kings and been blessed by Melchizedek. Outwardly he is a man of success, but the promise on which he left everything has not begun: he has no child.

The reading then jumps over six chapters. It leaves out the covenant ceremony of 15:7–21, the story of Hagar and Ishmael, the covenant of circumcision and the visit at Mamre, and goes straight to the birth of Isaac.
str: 15:1: God speaks first: do not fear.
15:2–3: Abram's honest complaint: I am childless, and a servant of my house will inherit.
15:4–5: the answer: your own son; look at the stars.
15:6: Abram believes, and God counts it as righteousness.
21:1–3: God keeps his word: Sarah bears Isaac.
¶ The two passages are promise and fulfilment. Between them lie many years of waiting, which the Lectionary passes over in a moment, but which Abraham and Sarah lived day by day.
kw: From the same root as “Amen”. It means to lean on someone as firm and reliable. Abram does not see anything new in v. 6. He rests his weight on the one who has spoken.
In the Bible, to be righteous is to stand rightly in relationship with God. God counts Abram's trust as that right standing.
The verb of 21:1, which the NRSV renders “dealt with”. It often describes God coming in person to act for his people, as in Genesis 50:24 and Exodus 3:16.
The name is linked with the Hebrew for laughter. Both Abraham and Sarah had laughed at the promise (17:17; 18:12), and Sarah now laughs for joy (21:6).
vv: Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.
This is the first time in the Bible that God says “Do not be afraid”. It is said to a man who is weary of waiting, before he has said a word.
O Lord God, what will you give me, for I continue childless
Faith here is not silence. Abram tells God exactly what hurts. Many couples who long for a child, and many who have lost one, can pray with this verse.
Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
God brings Abram outside. Abram has been counting what he lacks, and God tells him to count something that cannot be counted.
And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.
One of the great verses of the Bible. St Paul builds on it in Romans 4 and Galatians 3, and James 2:23 quotes it too.
Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the time of which God had spoken to him.
Abraham is a hundred years old (21:5). The stress falls on God's fidelity: “as he had said”, “as he had promised”, “at the time of which God had spoken”.
ch: St Paul reads Genesis 15:6 as proof that God's people are made righteous through faith, and calls Abraham the father of all who believe (Romans 4:11). The Catechism says that Abraham fulfils the definition of faith given in Hebrews 11:1 (CCC 146) and adds that God's promise of descendants is “the fruit of faith and of the power of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 706). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the beginnings of the Church's faith and election are already found among the patriarchs, Moses and the prophets (Nostra Aetate 4). The Church is not ashamed of these roots; she gives thanks for them. In the Roman Canon the Mass itself names “the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith”.

r.h: He remembers his covenant for ever
set: Psalm 105 is a long hymn that tells Israel's history as the story of God's faithfulness: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Joseph in Egypt, Moses and the Exodus, and the gift of the land. Its first verses (vv. 1–15) appear again in 1 Chronicles 16:8–22, where they are sung when David brings the ark to Jerusalem. Today's verses take only the opening call to praise and the statement of the covenant with Abraham.
str: vv. 1–2: give thanks and tell the nations.
vv. 3–4: rejoice and seek the Lord.
vv. 5–6: remember, you children of Abraham and Jacob.
vv. 8–9: God himself remembers his covenant.
¶ The people are told to remember (v. 5) because God remembers first (v. 8). Israel's memory rests on the memory of God.
kw: This imperative opens the psalm. The verb also means to acknowledge, to declare openly what God has done.
When God “remembers” in the Bible he does not recall a forgotten fact. He acts on his promise, as in Genesis 8:1 and Exodus 2:24.
The binding bond God makes with his people. Psalm 105 uses it of the promise to Abraham, the same promise as today's first reading.
vv: O give thanks to the Lord, call on his name, make known his deeds among the peoples.
Even in the Old Testament, the story of Israel is meant to be told to the nations. Simeon will sing of the same horizon in today's Gospel.
Seek the Lord and his strength; seek his presence continually.
Literally “seek his face always”. To seek God is the work of a whole life, never something finished.
He is mindful of his covenant forever, of the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations,
A thousand generations is the Bible's way of saying without end. Compare Deuteronomy 7:9.
ch: Zechariah and Mary sing in the same key at the beginning of Luke's Gospel. God has remembered “his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our ancestor Abraham” (Luke 1:72–73), and Mary too ends her song with Abraham (Luke 1:54–55). St Augustine, in his work On the Trinity, returns to the words “seek his face always” as a motto for the whole search for God (in substance). On this feast the psalm tells parents that they hand on a memory: the deeds of God, told from one generation to the next.

r.h: By faith Abraham obeyed
set: Hebrews is a sermon to tired Christians, probably of Jewish background; its author is not named. Chapter 11 opens with a definition: “faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1). A long roll of witnesses follows, from Abel to the martyrs, each introduced by the same words “by faith”. Abraham has more space than anyone. The reading selects three moments: his call, the birth of a son, and the test on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22).
str: v. 8: the call: he leaves without knowing where he is going.
vv. 11–12: the child: from a man as good as dead come descendants like the stars.
vv. 17–19: the test: he is ready to offer the son of the promise.
¶ Each step asks more. First Abraham gives up his past, then he trusts God for his future, and finally he is ready to give back the future God has given him.
kw: The one word that opens each example in the chapter, like a drumbeat. It stands first in the Greek for emphasis.
Used of Isaac in v. 17, although Abraham also had Ishmael. It marks Isaac as the unique child of the promise. John uses the same word of Christ (John 1:14, 18).
Literally “in a parable”. Isaac did not die, so his return was not a true resurrection, yet it points forward to one.
vv: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out, not knowing where he was going.
Abraham knew who was calling him, even though he did not know the destination. Faith does not need the whole map.
because he considered him faithful who had promised.

A note on the text. The Greek of this verse is difficult, and translators differ on who is the subject. The NRSV makes Abraham the one who received power to beget; the Malayalam POC, like many older versions, makes Sarah the one who received power to conceive. Either way, the ground of faith is the same: the one who promised is faithful.
He considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead
Here is the most striking comment on Genesis 22. Abraham could not see how the promise would survive, but he trusted that God could raise the dead. This is faith at its fullest.
figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
The Church has always seen here an image of Christ's death and resurrection.
ch: The Catechism presents Abraham's sacrifice as the last stage in the purification of his faith, and says that the father of believers is thus made like the Father who will not spare his own Son (CCC 2572; compare CCC 145–147). St Irenaeus teaches that Abraham, in his faith, readily gave up his only and beloved son so that God might also give his own Son for us (in substance, Against Heresies 4.5). For parents the passage is demanding and consoling: to hand a child over to God is the highest act of faith, and God does not take what is given to him in order to destroy it.

r.h: They brought him up to present him to the Lord
set: Forty days after the birth of a son, a Jewish mother came to the Temple for the rite of purification. She brought a lamb and a bird, or two birds if she could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:2–8). Separately, every firstborn son belonged to the Lord (Exodus 13:2, 12) and was bought back with a payment (Numbers 18:16).

Luke weaves these customs into one scene. He speaks of “their” purification, and he says nothing of a payment. He shows the child being given to God, as Hannah gave Samuel at the sanctuary (1 Samuel 1:24–28). Five times in this passage Luke mentions the law (2:22, 23, 24, 27, 39). The family of Jesus is a devout Jewish family, living by the Torah. The shorter form of the Gospel keeps only the arrival and the return to Nazareth.
str: vv. 22–24: Mary and Joseph bring the child and the offering of the poor.
vv. 25–28: Simeon, led by the Spirit, takes the child in his arms.
vv. 29–32: his song: a light for the Gentiles, glory for Israel.
vv. 33–35: the second word: a sign opposed, and a sword for Mary.
vv. 36–38: Anna gives thanks and speaks about the child.
vv. 39–40: home to Nazareth, where the child grows.
kw: The word for bringing someone before a superior, and also for presenting an offering. Jesus enters the Temple as one who is offered.
What Simeon awaits (v. 25). It recalls “Comfort, O comfort my people” in Isaiah 40:1. Jewish hope is met in a child.
A large sword. Simeon's word sets the shadow of the Cross over Mary's joy, in the middle of the Christmas season.
vv: they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord
Malachi 3:1 had said that the Lord would suddenly come to his Temple. He comes, carried in his parents' arms, and hardly anyone notices.
a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.

This is the offering of those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8). The Son of God grew up in a family of modest means. St Paul's words fit: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).
Simeon took him in his arms and praised God
Mary and Joseph let a stranger take their child in his arms. A family that holds its child with open hands lets others meet him.
a sword will pierce your own soul too.
Mary does not stand outside the drama of her Son. The pain of a mother is included in his mission.
The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom; and the favor of God was upon him.
Luke says almost the same of John the Baptist (1:80) and of the boy Samuel (1 Samuel 2:21, 26). The eternal Son truly grows, day by day, in a home at Nazareth, among his relatives and neighbours.
ch: The Catechism sees in this scene the firstborn Son who belongs to the Lord, and says that Simeon's sword announces Christ's perfect oblation on the cross (CCC 529). Vatican II says that the union of the Mother with her Son in the work of salvation appears here (Lumen Gentium 57). On Nazareth, the Catechism teaches that the hidden life lets every person meet Jesus in the most ordinary events of daily life (CCC 533), and it quotes St Paul VI's address at Nazareth on the lessons of silence, family life and work. Christ chose to be born and grow up in a family, and so the Christian home is called the domestic church (CCC 1655–1657; Lumen Gentium 11). St John Chrysostom told his people to make the home a little church (in substance, Homilies on Ephesians 20).

qa: Why are there different readings for this feast?

The Lectionary gives Sirach 3 and Colossians 3 as readings that may be used in every year, and it also offers proper readings for Years A, B and C. Today's are those of Year B. A parish that hears Sirach and Colossians is keeping the same feast.
Mary was without sin. Why did she need purification?

Purification in Leviticus 12 concerns ritual purity after childbirth, not moral guilt. Mary and Joseph keep the law as faithful Jews, and her Son himself was “born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). Their obedience is an act of devotion, not an admission of sin.
Luke calls Joseph the child's father. Does that deny the virgin birth?

No. Luke has already told of the virginal conception (1:34–35). Joseph was truly the head of the household and the father who cared for Jesus, gave him his name and his place in the house of David. St John Paul II reflects on this fatherhood in Redemptoris Custos.
Was the Holy Family perfect, so that my family cannot compare?

They were holy, but their life was not easy. They knew poverty, a birth away from home, and a word about a sword. Pope Francis points to this real family in Amoris Laetitia 65–66. Their holiness lay in trust and in love, and every family can learn these.
rite: The devotion to the Holy Family grew in the nineteenth century. Pope Leo XIII promoted it, and Pope Benedict XV extended the feast to the whole Latin Church in 1921. The Roman calendar of 1969 placed it on the Sunday within the Octave of Christmas, so that the mystery of the home at Nazareth is kept in the light of the crib. Because 27 December is a Sunday this year, the feast of St John the Apostle gives way to it. The Presentation itself has its own feast on 2 February, when candles are blessed. St Sophronius of Jerusalem preached on that day that all should run to meet Christ with lights in their hands (in substance). The whole Mass of today is an invitation for each family to bring its children, and its worries, to the altar.
study: When has my family had to wait a long time for something God seemed to have promised? What did we say to him in that time?
Abraham left “not knowing where he was going”. What decision in our home is asking for that kind of trust just now?
Mary and Joseph offer the offering of the poor. What small thing can our family truly offer to God this week?
Jesus grew up in the ordinary life of Nazareth. Which ordinary part of our day could become a place of prayer?

lead: Three days after Christmas the Church wears red and remembers the children of Bethlehem. The readings do not soften the contrast. John's letter proclaims that “God is light” and that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin, yet it knows that darkness is real and that people walk in it. The psalm is the song of those who have escaped by God's help alone. Matthew tells of a king who, out of fear for his throne, kills children, while Joseph carries the child away by night and Rachel weeps. The key words are light, blood and weeping. The Church does not explain away this grief. She sets it beside the crib and the Cross.

r.h: God is light, and the blood of Jesus cleanses us
set: The First Letter of John does not name its author; tradition links it with St John and the community formed by his Gospel. It is usually dated toward the end of the first century. A division has torn that community: some have gone out (2:19) and seem to claim knowledge of God while denying that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (4:2) and making light of sin and of love for others.

The Lectionary reads this letter through the days of Christmas. It suits the season: the same voice that says “the Word became flesh” here says what that means for daily life. Today's passage follows straight after the opening verses (1:1–4).
str: 1:5: the message: God is light.
1:6–7: first false claim, and the true way: walking in the light.
1:8–9: second false claim: “we have no sin”; the true way: confession.
1:10: third false claim: “we have not sinned”.
2:1–2: the remedy: Jesus Christ, advocate and atoning sacrifice.
¶ The pattern “If we say… ” repeats. John measures words against life. He writes neither to excuse sin nor to crush the sinner.
kw: A real sharing of life. In John it runs in two directions at once: with God and “with one another” (1:7).
One called alongside to speak for another, as a defender in court. John's Gospel uses it of the Holy Spirit (John 14:16); here it is used of Jesus.
The offering by which sin is taken away and the relationship restored. The word occurs in the New Testament only in this letter (2:2; 4:10), where the source is God's own love.
vv: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
The verb is in the present tense: it cleanses, again and again. Today of all days the words sound strong. The blood of the Innocents is shed because of Christ; the blood of Christ is shed for them.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
Christians can still sin, and denying it is its own kind of darkness. St Augustine often quoted this verse against those who taught that the baptized could live without any sin (in substance).
If we confess our sins, he who is faithful and just will forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
God is “just” here because he keeps his promise to forgive. To confess is to say the same as God says about my sin.
My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.
John's tone is that of an old pastor. His first goal is that they not sin; the second half of the verse then gives hope to those who do.
and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
The horizon is the whole world. John's little community may not think of Christ as its private possession.
ch: The Catechism uses 1:5 when it teaches that God is truth (CCC 214), quotes 1:8–9 on conversion and the mercy of God (CCC 1425, 1847), and quotes 2:2 for the Church's teaching that Christ died for all without exception (CCC 605). St Augustine, who preached a series of homilies on this letter, says that its chief message is love (in substance). In the Mass we confess our sins at the start, and we hear the Lamb “who takes away the sins of the world” before Communion: the same two movements as this passage.

r.h: The snare is broken, and we have escaped
set: Psalm 124 is one of the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134), sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. Its title links it with David. It is a thanksgiving of the whole people after a danger that would have destroyed them. No particular event is named, so it can be sung in any age.
str: vv. 2–3: if the Lord had not been with us, they would have swallowed us alive.
vv. 4–5: the flood would have swept over us.
vv. 7b–8: the snare is broken; our help is in the Lord's name.
¶ Three images of danger, a beast with open jaws, a flood and a hunter's trap, are each answered by the one fact that God was on their side.
kw: A small, helpless creature. Israel sees itself in such a bird: it has no strength of its own.
A trap for birds. The psalm does not say that the bird broke it. The snare “is broken”, by another.
The same language as Psalm 121:2. The maker of heaven and earth is the one who helps.
vv: if it had not been the Lord who was on our side, when our enemies attacked us,
The whole psalm hangs on this “if”. The singer looks back and sees how near the end was.
then the flood would have swept us away, the torrent would have gone over us;
In the Bible, great waters are the image of chaos and death, as with Jonah 2:3 and Psalm 69:1–2.
the snare is broken, and we have escaped.
Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.
One of the best-known verses in Christian prayer.
ch: The Church sings this psalm today on behalf of children who did not escape from Herod's sword. So it has to be heard at a deeper level. Their escape is of another kind, for the Church holds that they have been taken into Christ's victory, beyond the reach of every snare. The Mass of the day has long applied the image of the bird to them. V. 8 has entered the liturgy: “Our help is in the name of the Lord” is the versicle with which many blessings in the Roman Rite begin.

r.h: Rachel weeping for her children
set: In Matthew's first two chapters, each scene is built around a passage of the prophets, and he repeats a formula of fulfilment. Today there are two such quotations, Hosea and Jeremiah. The Magi have just left by another road. Joseph, who is silent throughout the Gospels, receives the second of his dreams (1:20; 2:13, 19, 22).

Herod the Great ruled Judea under Rome and died in 4 BC. The Jewish historian Josephus records his brutality toward any rival, including the killing of a wife and of his own sons. Josephus does not mention Bethlehem, but the deed fits what he tells of Herod. Bethlehem was a small place, and commentators often estimate that the children killed were perhaps a dozen or two. Matthew is not reporting a statistic; every one of them was somebody's child. Egypt was a natural place of refuge, with large Jewish communities at that time.
str: vv. 13–14: the dream, and the night journey.
v. 15: first fulfilment: “Out of Egypt I have called my son”.
v. 16: Herod's rage and the killing of the children.
vv. 17–18: second fulfilment: Rachel weeps at Ramah.

¶ The whole passage retells the story of Moses. A cruel king kills male children (Exodus 1:22), and one child is saved, flees, and returns when those who sought his life are dead (Exodus 4:19; Matthew 2:20).
kw: Joseph is repeatedly told to take “the child and his mother” (2:13, 20). The phrase shows his place: he has charge of them, and the two are always named together.
to trick, to make a fool of
Herod feels that the Magi have mocked him. The later Passion uses the same verb of the soldiers mocking Jesus (27:29). Pride wounded is the root of Herod's violence.
Not merely a prediction coming true. God's earlier works with Israel, in Egypt and in exile, reach a fullness in Jesus.
vv: Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt
The Son of God begins his life on earth as a refugee, and the Church's concern for migrants has a root here.
Then Joseph got up, took the child and his mother by night, and went to Egypt,
No word is spoken, and no question is asked. Joseph obeys at once, in the dark.
Out of Egypt I have called my son.
Hosea 11:1 speaks of Israel coming out of Egypt. Matthew sees Jesus living through his people's history in his own person. Jesus is God's Son in a unique sense.
he sent and killed all the children in and around Bethlehem who were two years old or under
The evil here belongs to one man who feared for his power. Matthew does not blame the people of Judea, who are the victims. It is a warning about what power will do when it feels itself threatened.
A voice was heard in Ramah, wailing and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children;

Jeremiah 31:15 pictures Rachel, mother of the northern tribes, weeping as the exiles pass on the way to Babylon; Ramah was a gathering place for the exiles (Jeremiah 40:1). Another tradition placed her tomb on the way to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19). The next verses in Jeremiah offer comfort: “there is hope for your future” (31:17). Matthew leaves the promise unspoken here. It will come at Easter.
ch: The Catechism says that the flight into Egypt and the massacre of the innocents show the opposition of darkness to the light, that Christ's whole life was lived under the sign of persecution, and that his own share it with him (CCC 530). These children did not know Christ and were not baptized with water, yet the Church has honoured them since ancient times as martyrs, because they died for his sake (compare CCC 1258, on the baptism of blood). St Irenaeus says that the Lord sent them ahead into his kingdom (in substance, Against Heresies 3.16). St Quodvultdeus, in the sermon in today's Office of Readings, marvels that children who cannot yet speak bear witness to Christ (in substance), and the poet Prudentius greets them as “flowers of the martyrs”. The Church teaches that all innocent human life is sacred from conception (CCC 2270), and today she remembers all children who suffer from war, neglect and violence.

qa: Did this really happen, since no other ancient writer mentions it?

Matthew is the only source. Josephus does not mention it, but the killing of a few village children may have seemed small beside Herod's other crimes, and it matches what is known of his character. The Church has kept the feast as a real event, while Matthew's main concern is the meaning of the event in God's plan.
Why did God warn Joseph but not the other parents?

Scripture does not answer this, and we should not invent an answer. The passage gives no explanation. It gives Rachel's weeping, which is a prayer, and it shows God's Son himself entering a world where such things happen, on his way to a Cross where he too will be killed unjustly. The answer to innocent suffering in Christian faith is less an argument than the crucified and risen Lord.
How can the unbaptized children be saints?

The Church has long regarded those who die for Christ before baptism as baptized by their death (CCC 1258). The Innocents are the first example honoured in the liturgy. Scripture says nothing of their number or their names, and the Church honours them with one feast.
rite: In the Roman calendar the Innocents stand close behind Christmas with St Stephen on 26 December and St John on 27 December. An old way of speaking, found in St Bernard, explains the three together: Stephen was a martyr in will and in deed, John in will, and the Innocents in deed (in substance). Red vestments mark the feast as a feast of martyrs. It is a fitting day to pray for parents who have lost a child, for children who are in danger, and for the protection of every unborn child, and to bring those names to the altar at Mass.
study: John says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” Where do I find it hardest to tell the truth about myself before God?
Herod killed because he feared losing his place. What am I most afraid of losing, and how does that fear affect the people around me?
Joseph obeyed by night without knowing the road. What does trust look like when I cannot see the outcome?
How can our parish or family stand by a mother or father who, like Rachel, refuses to be consoled?

lead: Both readings today speak of light that has already begun to shine. John says that “the true light is already shining”, and tests the claim by a simple question: do you love your brother or sister? Simeon holds the child and calls him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles”. The light of Christmas is real, and it asks to be lived.

r.h: Whoever loves lives in the light
set: John continues to test the claims of those who say that they know God. Knowing God, for him, cannot be separated from obeying him and from loving others. He gives three tests: keeping the commandments, walking as Jesus walked, and love of one's brother or sister.
str: vv. 3–6: to know him is to keep his word and to walk as he walked.
vv. 7–8: the commandment is both old and new.
vv. 9–11: love is light; hatred is darkness and blindness.
kw: In the Bible, knowing God is a lived relationship, not just having information. John uses the word many times in this letter.
Old, because they had it from the beginning; new, because Christ gave it a new measure (John 13:34): “as I have loved you”.
Literally a trap or an obstacle on the path. One who loves can see the road, and does not trip himself or others.
vv: whoever says, “I abide in him,” ought to walk just as he walked.
The test is plain. On the fifth day of Christmas it asks what we have seen at the crib: humility, poverty and self-gift are the way he walked.
because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
The world still has darkness in it, but the change has begun, as with the first light before sunrise.
Whoever loves a brother or sister lives in the light, and in such a person there is no cause for stumbling.
The Greek says “brother”. The NRSV rightly makes clear that this takes in everyone in the community, men and women alike.
ch: St Augustine, in his homilies on this letter, says that love alone distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John 5). The Catechism says that the law of the People of God is the new commandment to love as Christ loved us (CCC 782).

r.h: My eyes have seen your salvation
set: This is the first part of the scene in the Temple, read in full on the feast of the Holy Family. Today the attention falls on Simeon. Luke tells us nothing about his office and does not say that he was old, although v. 29 suggests it. Three times Luke mentions the Holy Spirit in connection with him (vv. 25, 26, 27), and the Spirit, who led the prophets, is at work again in Israel.
str: vv. 22–24: the parents fulfil the law.
vv. 25–28: Simeon is led to the child.
vv. 29–32: the song known as the Nunc Dimittis.
vv. 33–35: the sign and the sword.
kw: The word a slave uses to his owner. Simeon speaks to God as a servant to his Master.
The word for releasing a servant from duty. Simeon's watch is over, and he may go off duty at peace.
A sign that people will argue over and reject. Jesus forces a decision, and hearts are shown for what they are.
vv: he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Messiah.
A whole life was shaped by this one promise, and it was kept quietly, one day after another.
Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word;
The Church prays this song every night at Night Prayer. It is the prayer of someone who can lay the day down, because God has kept his word.
for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.
The words echo Isaiah 42:6, 49:6 and 52:10. Christ is light for the nations, and he remains the glory of Israel. Neither takes the place of the other.
This child is destined for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be opposed
Compare Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16, the stone on which some stumble and others build. This is a word about every human heart, spoken in Israel first because the Gospel comes to Israel first.
ch: Vatican II opens its great Constitution on the Church with the same title of Christ: “Christ is the Light of nations” (Lumen Gentium 1). The Catechism notes that with Simeon and Anna all Israel awaits its encounter with the Savior (CCC 529). Origen tells his hearers that if they want to hold Jesus in their arms, they must let the Spirit lead them, as Simeon did, into God's temple (in substance, Homilies on Luke 15).

qa: Does “the falling and the rising of many in Israel” mean that God has rejected the Jewish people?

No. The Church firmly rejects that view (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). Simeon, Anna, Mary, Joseph and the first disciples are all from Israel, and the same song calls the child Israel's glory. The words are about the decision that Christ asks of every person, and they apply no less to Christians.
rite: Today the Roman calendar allows an optional memorial of St Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, who was killed in his cathedral on 29 December 1170 after a long dispute with King Henry II over the rights of the Church. Like Simeon's child, he became a sign that was opposed. He is remembered in the Octave of Christmas, near St Stephen and the Innocents.
study: John's test is love of the brother or sister I actually have. Who is the person in my life who shows up how much light I really walk in?
Simeon says, “now you are dismissing your servant in peace.” What would I need to put right to be able to pray this at the end of today?

lead: John writes to the whole community, young and old, to remind them of what they already have: forgiveness, knowledge of God, strength against evil. Then he warns them not to set their hearts on what is passing away. Luke shows us someone who has done exactly that. Anna, a widow of great age, has given her life to God in the Temple, and she is ready when the child comes.

r.h: Those who do the will of God live forever
set: The passage falls into two parts. A short, almost poetic section addresses the believers as children, fathers and young people, and is full of encouragement. A sharp warning follows about love of “the world”. Encouragement comes first, because John is not writing to people who are lost.
str: vv. 12–14: to children, fathers and young people: what grace has already done in you.
vv. 15–16: do not love the world; three desires.
v. 17: the world passes, but the one who does God's will remains.
kw: In John the word has more than one sense. God loves the world (John 3:16). Here it means human life organized without God and against him, not creation, which is good.
Desire that has gone astray, which grasps and possesses. The tradition speaks of concupiscence.
Literally “pride of life”, where bios can mean one's life or one's means of living. It is the boasting of those who rely on what they have. The Malayalam POC reads the pride of life.
vv: I write to you, young people, because you are strong and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
John first tells the young what is true of them. Their strength lies in the word of God that lives in them, and not in their own force.
the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, the pride in riches
Many commentators compare the tree in Genesis 3:6, which was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desired to make one wise.
And the world and its desire are passing away, but those who do the will of God live forever.
On the second-last day of the calendar year this is a good sentence to read slowly. Whatever is done for God stays.
ch: The Catechism names these three desires when it speaks of the harmony lost by sin (CCC 377) and explains that St John distinguishes three kinds of covetousness or concupiscence (CCC 2514). The Church does not despise the world God made. Vatican II says plainly that Christians are to work in the world and order it toward God (Lumen Gentium 31). The warning is about where the heart rests.

r.h: She began to speak about the child
set: Luke likes to set a woman next to a man: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna. Two witnesses are given, as the law asked (Deuteronomy 19:15). Anna is of the tribe of Asher, a northern tribe. Her presence means that the whole of Israel, even from the scattered tribes, is present in the Temple to greet the child.
str: vv. 36–37: who Anna is: prophet, widow, a woman of prayer.
v. 38: her praise and her word to others.
vv. 39–40: the return to Nazareth and the growth of the child.

¶ A note on the text. The Greek of v. 37 can mean that she was eighty-four years old, as the NRSV and the POC take it, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years. The point is the same: a long life given to God.
kw: Anna stands in the line of Miriam, Deborah and Huldah. Her prophecy is simply to recognize the child and speak about him.
With prayer, the mark of her daily life. Compare the widow Judith (Judith 8:4–6) and 1 Timothy 5:5.
The buying back of what was lost or enslaved. Those around her long for God to come and restore Jerusalem (Isaiah 52:9).
vv: There was also a prophet, Anna the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher.
Her name is the Hebrew Hannah, the mother of Samuel, and it comes from a root meaning grace or favour. Phanuel means “face of God”. Beyond this brief notice, nothing more is known of her.
She never left the temple but worshiped there with fasting and prayer night and day.
Not a wasted old age. A life of prayer was the hidden preparation for this one moment, of which she could not have known the date.
At that moment she came, and began to praise God and to speak about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.
Her words are not recorded. She finds those who are waiting and tells them. This is the simplest form of evangelization.
When they had finished everything required by the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth.
The Son of God goes back to thirty hidden years. God's great work continues in a small town.
ch: The Catechism says that with Simeon and Anna all Israel awaits its encounter with the Savior (CCC 529). Since apostolic times the Church has honoured Christian widows and virgins who, called by the Lord to cling only to him, have given their lives to God (CCC 922). In every parish there are Annas, elderly people of daily Mass and the rosary, and their prayer holds up more than we can see.

qa: Luke has the family go back to Nazareth. Where is the flight into Egypt that Matthew tells of?

Each Evangelist selects his material for his own purpose. Luke does not mention Egypt, and Matthew does not mention the Presentation. The Gospels do not give a complete timetable of these years, and the Church has not bound us to one way of fitting them together. Both accounts teach the same faith.
study: John tells the young they are strong because the word of God abides in them. What word of God has remained in me through the changes of this past year?
Who is the Anna in my parish or family, and have I ever told them what their prayer means?

lead: On the last day of the calendar year the Church reads of an end and of a beginning. John says, “it is the last hour”, and reminds his community that they already have what they need: the anointing and the truth. The Gospel goes back before all time: “In the beginning was the Word”, and then comes down to one point in history, “the Word became flesh”. Every year ends. The Word does not.

r.h: You have been anointed by the Holy One
set: The crisis behind the letter comes into the open here. A group has left the community, and John does not hide how serious this is. For him it is a sign of the last times. Yet he writes to reassure those who remain and not to frighten them.
str: v. 18: the last hour, and the many antichrists.
v. 19: those who went out.
vv. 20–21: you are anointed, and you know the truth.
kw: The time opened by Christ's coming, death and resurrection. It does not give a date. It describes the whole age of the Church, lived in the light of his return.
In the New Testament the word occurs only in 1 and 2 John (2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7). The first meaning is one who opposes Christ by denying him. John says that many have already come.

The word occurs in the New Testament only in this passage (2:20, 27). It probably points to the Holy Spirit, and perhaps to the word received at baptism. “Christ” and “Christian” come from the same root.
vv: Children, it is the last hour! As you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come.

The Greek has “antichrist” both times; the Malayalam POC reads “false christs” the second time. John is less concerned with one figure of the future than with those present in his time who deny Christ.
They went out from us, but they did not belong to us;

The pain of a divided Church is an old pain. John's words were written about one crisis in his own community. They do not give us the right to pass judgment on Christians of other Churches today, whom Vatican II calls brothers and sisters (Unitatis Redintegratio 3).
But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and all of you have knowledge.

A note on the text. Some ancient manuscripts read “all of you have knowledge”, which the NRSV follows; others read “you know all things”, the reading of the Latin Vulgate. The first seems to fit John's point: knowledge is not for a special group, as some may have claimed, but for all the anointed.
ch: The Catechism teaches that before Christ's second coming the Church will pass through a final trial, and that the supreme religious deception is that of the Antichrist (CCC 675). It warns against false hopes of a messianic age within history (CCC 676). Catholics are anointed with sacred chrism after baptism and at confirmation, as a sign of sharing in the anointing of Christ (CCC 1241, 1294).

r.h: The Word became flesh
set: These verses open the Fourth Gospel and they are also the Gospel of the Mass during the day on Christmas. Their poetic form has led many scholars to think of them as a hymn, into which the Evangelist has placed the verses on John the Baptist (vv. 6–8, 15). The opening words echo Genesis 1:1. A new creation is being told.
str: vv. 1–5: the Word with God, the Word as creator, life and light.
vv. 6–8: John the witness.
vv. 9–13: the light comes into the world; some receive him and become children of God.
vv. 14–18: the Word became flesh; grace upon grace; the Son makes the Father known.

¶ A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts had no punctuation. The NRSV ends the sentence at “not one thing came into being” and begins the next with “What has come into being”. The POC reads differently at this point. The sense of the passage is not affected.
kw: In the Old Testament God creates by his word (Genesis 1; Psalm 33:6), and wisdom is with God from the beginning (Proverbs 8:22–31). John uses the word of a Person who is with God and who is God.
Not a body alone but human nature in its weakness and mortality. John chooses a strong word on purpose. The Church's word “Incarnation” comes from this verse (CCC 461).
Literally “pitched his tent”. It recalls the tent of meeting, where God's glory dwelt among Israel (Exodus 40:34). Christ's body is now the place where God dwells among us.
vv: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Three short statements: the Word's eternity, his distinction from the Father, and his divinity. The whole later teaching of the Council of Nicaea is in seed here.
And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father’s only son, full of grace and truth.
The centre of the Prologue and the reason for Christmas. “Grace and truth” probably echoes the Hebrew pair ḥesed and ’ĕmet, steadfast love and faithfulness, of Exodus 34:6.
No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known.

A note on the text. The oldest Greek manuscripts read “God the only Son”, which the NRSV and the POC follow; many others read “the only Son”. Either way, the Son alone makes the Father known, and in Jesus we see the Father (John 14:9).
ch: The Catechism devotes a section to why the Word became flesh: to save us by reconciling us with God, so that we might know God's love, to be our model of holiness, and to make us “partakers of the divine nature” (CCC 456–460). It quotes St Athanasius: the Son of God became man so that we might become God (CCC 460). In the older form of the Roman Mass these verses were read at the end of almost every Mass as the “Last Gospel”. The Angelus still repeats v. 14 three times a day.

qa: “His own people did not accept him” (1:11). Is this a charge against the Jewish people?

No. It describes the drama of every human heart that closes itself to God, and the same chapter goes on to speak of those who did receive him. Mary, Joseph, John the Baptist and the apostles were all Jews. The Church rejects any blame placed on the Jewish people as a whole (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
rite: Today has an optional memorial of St Sylvester I, pope from 314 to 335, who led the Church in the years after the persecutions ended. In the evening the Vigil Mass of the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, is celebrated. It is an old Latin custom to sing the Te Deum in thanksgiving on the last day of the year, and the Church grants a plenary indulgence, under the usual conditions, to those who take part in its public recitation today.
study: John says “it is the last hour.” How would I spend tonight if I took those words seriously and without fear?
Looking back on this year, where did I see the Word made flesh among us, in a person, in an event, in the Mass?
